knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty closed set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\bar x\in C\), the contingent tangent cone is
\[T_C(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\frac{d(\bar x+t v,C)}{t}=0\right\}.\]
Thus a direction is contingent when arbitrarily small positive steps along it can be corrected by an error of order \(o(t)\) to reach \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The contingent cone contains directions along which arbitrarily small positive steps approach the set with error negligible relative to the step size.
knowledge_statements.title: Contingent Tangency

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Bouligand tangent cone to \(C\) at \(\bar x\) is
\[T_C^B(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists\,t_k\downarrow0,\ \exists\,x_k\in C,\ \frac{x_k-\bar x}{t_k}\to v\right\}.\]
Equivalently, one may require vectors \(v_k\to v\) with \(\bar x+t_kv_k\in C\). In finite dimensions this cone equals the contingent cone \(T_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Bouligand tangent is the limit of rescaled feasible displacements. In finite dimensions this sequential cone is the contingent tangent cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The principal sequential variants are
\[T_C(\bar x)=\mathop{\mathrm{Limsup}}_{t\downarrow0}\frac{C-\bar x}{t},\qquad T_C^A(\bar x)=\mathop{\mathrm{Liminf}}_{t\downarrow0}\frac{C-\bar x}{t}.\]
Accordingly, \(v\in T_C(\bar x)\) requires some sequence \(t_k\downarrow0\) and some \(v_k\to v\) with \(\bar x+t_kv_k\in C\). By contrast, \(v\in T_C^A(\bar x)\) requires such correcting vectors \(v_k\to v\) for every prescribed sequence \(t_k\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outer-limit tangency uses some vanishing scale sequence, whereas inner-limit tangency must work along every prescribed vanishing scale sequence.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Tangency Variants

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The adjacent tangent cone to \(C\) at \(\bar x\) is
\[T_C^A(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\forall\,t_k\downarrow0\ \exists\,v_k\to v\text{ such that }\bar x+t_kv_k\in C\right\}.\]
Equivalently, \(d(\bar x+t v,C)/t\to0\) as \(t\downarrow0\). Since persistence for every vanishing scale implies existence along some scale, \(T_C^A(\bar x)\subset T_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adjacent tangent remains approximately feasible along every prescribed sequence of positive step sizes, so every adjacent tangent is contingent.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\bar x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T_C^{\mathrm{in}}(\bar x)=\left\{v:\exists\,\varepsilon,\delta>0\ \forall\,t\in(0,\delta),\ \forall\,w\in v+\varepsilon\mathbb B,\ \bar x+t w\in C\right\}.\]

notation.meaning: inner tangent cone under the uniform-neighborhood convention

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: uniform directional-neighborhood definition commonly called the inner or hypertangent cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the uniform-neighborhood convention, also called hypertangency in some texts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the uniform-neighborhood convention, the inner tangent cone is
\[T_C^{\mathrm{in}}(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists\,\varepsilon>0,\ \exists\,\delta>0\ \text{such that }\bar x+t w\in C\ \forall\,t\in(0,\delta),\ \forall\,w\in v+\varepsilon\mathbb B\right\}.\]
Thus feasibility persists simultaneously under all sufficiently small positive steps and all sufficiently small directional perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inner tangent has a whole neighborhood of nearby directions whose sufficiently short rays from the reference point remain feasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Inner Tangency

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniform directional-neighborhood construction is commonly called a hypertangent or strict feasible-direction construction, while “inner tangent cone” is also used for other objects. An authoritative source with a precise definition is required to establish the convention intended by this leaf.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Clarke tangent cone to \(C\) at \(\bar x\) is
\[T_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\forall\,x_k\to_C\bar x,\ \forall\,t_k\downarrow0\ \exists\,v_k\to v\text{ with }x_k+t_kv_k\in C\right\}.\]
It is a closed convex cone and satisfies \(T_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(\bar x)\subset T_C^A(\bar x)\subset T_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Clarke tangent remains approximately feasible under simultaneous perturbations of the base point and step size; the resulting cone is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Clarke Tangency

source_witnesses.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent finite-dimensional robust-distance formulation of Clarke tangency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A vector \(v\in\mathbb R^n\) belongs to the Clarke tangent cone exactly when
\[
\lim_{\substack{x\to\bar x,\ x\in C\\t\downarrow0}}\frac{d_C(x+tv)}{t}=0.
\]
Equivalently, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there are a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(\delta>0\) such that
\[
d_C(x+tv)\le\varepsilon t
\quad\text{for all }x\in C\cap U\text{ and }0<t<\delta.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Clarke tangent has uniformly negligible first-order feasibility error for every nearby base point and every sufficiently small positive step.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and closed.
\(\bar x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\in T_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(\bar x)\iff \lim_{x\to_C\bar x,\,t\downarrow0}d_C(x+tv)/t=0\).

children.title: Radial Cones
children.top_down_role: Feasible rays generated directly from the reference point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between two radial-cone conventions on a nonconvex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C:=\{0\}\cup\{1/k:k\in\mathbb N\}\subset\mathbb R\) and \(\bar x=0\). Then \[\operatorname{cone}(C-\bar x)=\mathbb R_+,\qquad \{v:\exists\delta>0\ \forall t\in[0,\delta],\ \bar x+tv\in C\}=\{0\}.\] Thus the conic-displacement and whole-short-ray conventions need not agree for a nonconvex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a sequence accumulating at zero, the conic-displacement cone is the nonnegative ray, whereas the whole-short-ray cone is only zero.
assumptions_latex: \(C=\{0\}\cup\{1/k:k\in\mathbb N\}\subset\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cone}(C-\bar x)=\mathbb R_+\) while the whole-short-ray cone equals \(\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Short-Ray and Conic-Displacement Conventions Differ

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\bar x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[R_C(\bar x)=\{v:\exists\,\delta>0\ \forall\,t\in[0,\delta],\ \bar x+t v\in C\}.\]

notation.meaning: radial feasible-direction cone to C at the reference point

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard feasible-direction version of the radial cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the short feasible-ray convention for radial directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The radial cone to \(C\) at \(\bar x\) is
\[R_C(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists\,\delta>0\text{ such that }\bar x+t v\in C\ \forall\,t\in[0,\delta]\right\}.\]
Every radial direction is contingent, so \(R_C(\bar x)\subset T_C(\bar x)\). If \(C\) is convex, then \(R_C(\bar x)=\operatorname{cone}(C-\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A radial direction generates a short feasible ray from the reference point. For convex sets, radial directions are precisely conic feasible displacements.
knowledge_statements.title: Radial Cones

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula defines directions whose entire sufficiently short ray is feasible. Many standard references instead define the radial cone as \(\operatorname{cone}(C-\bar x)\), which only requires one feasible positive displacement for a general nonconvex set. A source is needed to confirm the intended convention.

children.title: Linearized Cones
children.top_down_role: First-order constraint surrogates for feasible-direction geometry.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual representation of the active-gradient linearized cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the linearized cone of a finite differentiable constraint system at a feasible point \(\bar x\), \[L_C(\bar x)^\circ=\left\{\sum_{i\in I(\bar x)}\lambda_i\nabla g_i(\bar x)+\sum_{j=1}^p\mu_j\nabla h_j(\bar x):\lambda_i\ge0,\ \mu_j\in\mathbb R\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of the linearized cone is generated by nonnegative active-inequality gradients and arbitrary equality-gradient combinations.
assumptions_latex: \(g_i,h_j:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) are differentiable at the feasible point \(\bar x\).
\(L_C(\bar x)\) is the active-gradient linearized cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[L_C(\bar x)^\circ=\left\{\sum_{i\in I(\bar x)}\lambda_i\nabla g_i(\bar x)+\sum_j\mu_j\nabla h_j(\bar x):\lambda_i\ge0,\ \mu_j\in\mathbb R\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.title: Polar Multiplier Representation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral Structure of the Linearized Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite smooth equality-and-inequality constraint systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite differentiable constraint system at a feasible point \(\bar x\), the active-gradient linearized cone \(L_C(\bar x)\) is a closed convex polyhedral cone determined solely by the equality gradients and active inequality gradients at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The linearized cone is a closed convex polyhedral cone determined by the equality and active-inequality gradients.
assumptions_latex: \(g_i,h_j:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) are differentiable at \(\bar x\).
\(L_C(\bar x)\) is the active-gradient linearized cone of a finite constraint system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_C(\bar x)\) is a closed convex polyhedral cone determined by \(\{\nabla g_i(\bar x):i\in I(\bar x)\}\) and \(\{\nabla h_j(\bar x):1\le j\le p\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Structure of the Linearized Cone

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lineality Space of the Linearized Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural description of the active-gradient cone for a finite differentiable constraint system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the active-gradient linearized cone \(L_C(\bar x)\), \[\operatorname{lin}L_C(\bar x):=L_C(\bar x)\cap(-L_C(\bar x))=\left\{v:\nabla g_i(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}v=0\ \forall i\in I(\bar x),\ \nabla h_j(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}v=0\ \forall j\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reversible directions of the linearized cone are exactly those orthogonal to every active inequality gradient and every equality gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(g_i,h_j:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) are differentiable at the feasible point \(\bar x\).
\(L_C(\bar x)\) is the active-gradient linearized cone of the finite constraint system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{lin}L_C(\bar x)=\{v:\nabla g_i(\bar x)^\mathsf Tv=0\ (i\in I(\bar x)),\ \nabla h_j(\bar x)^\mathsf Tv=0\ (1\le j\le p)\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Lineality Space of the Linearized Cone

assumptions_latex: \(g_i,h_j:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) are differentiable at \(\bar x\).
\(C:=\{x:g_i(x)\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ h_j(x)=0\ (j=1,\ldots,p)\}\) and \(\bar x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[L_C(\bar x)=\{v:\nabla g_i(\bar x)^\top v\le0\ (i\in I(\bar x)),\ \nabla h_j(\bar x)^\top v=0\ (j=1,\ldots,p)\}.\]

notation.meaning: active inequality index set at the reference point
linearized cone of the constraint system

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard smooth nonlinear-programming linearized cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional equality-and-inequality constraint system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I(\bar x):=\{i:g_i(\bar x)=0\}\). The linearized cone of the constraint system at \(\bar x\) is
\[L_C(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\nabla g_i(\bar x)^\top v\le0\ \forall\,i\in I(\bar x),\ \nabla h_j(\bar x)^\top v=0\ \forall\,j\right\}.\]
Differentiability of the constraints yields the general inclusion \(T_C(\bar x)\subset L_C(\bar x)\); equality requires additional regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The linearized cone consists of directions satisfying the first-order active inequalities and equality equations. Every contingent tangent satisfies these linearized constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Linearized Cones

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The smooth finite-dimensional linearized cone and the inclusion \(T_C(\bar x)\subset L_C(\bar x)\) are standard and precisely stated, but no inspectable source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Linearization Exactness
children.top_down_role: Regularity regimes where linearized geometry recovers tangential geometry.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact radial, contingent, and linearized geometry for affine equality-and-inequality systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b,\ Hx=c\},\qquad \bar x\in C,\] and let \(R_C(\bar x)\) denote the feasible-ray cone \(\{v:\exists\delta>0,\ \bar x+t v\in C\ \forall t\in[0,\delta]\}\). With \(I(\bar x)=\{i:A_i\bar x=b_i\}\), \[R_C(\bar x)=T_C(\bar x)=L_C(\bar x)=\{v:A_i v\le0\ (i\in I(\bar x)),\ Hv=0\}.\] No additional constraint qualification is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a polyhedral constraint set, the feasible-ray, contingent, and active-constraint linearized cones coincide without an additional qualification.
assumptions_latex: \(C=\{x:Ax\le b,\ Hx=c\}\) and \(\bar x\in C\).
\(R_C(\bar x)=\{v:\exists\delta>0,\ \bar x+t v\in C\ \forall t\in[0,\delta]\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[R_C(\bar x)=T_C(\bar x)=L_C(\bar x)=\{v:A_i v\le0\ (i\in I(\bar x)),\ Hv=0\}.\]

notation.meaning: feasible-ray radial cone under the convention stated in the record

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Linearization Exactness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional nonlinear constraints under Mangasarian–Fromovitz regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C=\{x:g_i(x)\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ h_j(x)=0\ (j=1,\ldots,q)\},\] where the constraint functions are continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\in C\). Suppose the equality gradients are linearly independent and there exists \(d\) satisfying \[\nabla h_j(\bar x)^\top d=0\quad\forall j,\qquad \nabla g_i(\bar x)^\top d<0\quad\forall i\in I(\bar x).\] Then \[T_C(\bar x)=L_C(\bar x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mangasarian–Fromovitz regularity makes the active first-order linearization exact for the contingent cone.
assumptions_latex: The constraint functions are continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
The equality gradients at \(\bar x\) are linearly independent.
A direction strictly decreases every active inequality while satisfying the linearized equalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_C(\bar x)=L_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: MFCQ Tangent–Linearized Exactness

assumptions_latex: \(g_i\) and \(h_j\) are continuously differentiable near the feasible point \(\bar x\).
The vectors \(\nabla h_j(\bar x)\) are linearly independent.
There exists \(d\) with \(\nabla h_j(\bar x)^\top d=0\) for all \(j\) and \(\nabla g_i(\bar x)^\top d<0\) for every \(i\in I(\bar x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The proximal normal cone to \(C\) at \(\bar x\) is
\[N_C^P(\bar x):=\left\{\lambda(y-\bar x):\lambda\ge0,\ \bar x\in P_C(y)\right\}.\]
Equivalently, \(v\in N_C^P(\bar x)\) exactly when there exists \(\sigma\ge0\) such that
\[\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle\le\sigma\lVert x-\bar x\rVert^2\qquad\forall\,x\in C.\]
Thus a proximal normal is generated by a point having \(\bar x\) as a nearest point of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal normal points from a nearest point of the set toward an external point and equivalently satisfies a quadratic support inequality.

The Fréchet normal cone to \(C\) at \(\bar x\) is

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\) and any \(\bar x\in C\), all standard finite-dimensional normal cones coincide:
\[
\widehat N_C(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x)=N_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x)=N_C^{\mathrm{cvx}}(\bar x)
=\left\{v\in X:\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }x\in C\right\}.
\]
Thus neither sequential limiting nor Clarke convexification enlarges the normal cone when the underlying set is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex set, the Fréchet, limiting, Clarke, and classical convex normal cones all equal the global supporting cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Set Coincidence

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the coordinate cross \(C\) at \(\bar x=(0,0)\),
\[
N_C(\bar x)=(\mathbb R\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb R),
\]
whereas
\[
N_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}N_C(\bar x)=\mathbb R^2.

Therefore Clarke convexification fills every direction between the branchwise limiting normals. The strict inclusion \(N_C(\bar x)\subsetneq N_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x)\) identifies the information lost when a nonconvex normal cone is replaced by its closed convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two crossing axes, convexifying the limiting normals fills the entire plane and erases which normal directions came from individual branches.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a cone \(K\subset X\), define its negative polar by
\[
K^\circ:=\{v\in X:\langle v,w\rangle\le0\text{ for every }w\in K\}.
\]
If \(T_C(\bar x)\) denotes the Bouligand tangent cone, then the Fréchet normal cone has the representation
\[
\widehat N_C(\bar x)=T_C(\bar x)^\circ.
\]
Equivalently, \(v\) is Fréchet normal exactly when \(\langle v,w\rangle\le0\) for every tangent direction \(w\in T_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fréchet normal cone is exactly the negative polar of the Bouligand tangent cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Polar-Cone Representation

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the polar and dual cones by \[K^\circ:=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle y,x\rangle\leq 0\ \text{for every }x\in K\},\qquad K^*:=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle y,x\rangle\geq 0\ \text{for every }x\in K\}.\] Then changing the sign of the dual vector converts one representation into the other: \[K^*=-K^\circ.\] Both cones are closed and convex, even when \(K\) itself is neither closed nor convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual cone consists of vectors pairing nonnegatively with the original cone and equals the negative of its polar cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty cone \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(K^\circ:=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\ \text{for every }x\in K\}\). For any cones \(K_1,K_2\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), \(K_1\subset K_2\) implies \(K_2^\circ\subset K_1^\circ\). Moreover, \[K^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}K.\] Thus \(K^{\circ\circ}=K\) if and only if \(K\) is closed and convex, and polarity is an inclusion-reversing involution on the closed convex cones in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For Euclidean cones, polarity reverses inclusion, and applying it twice returns the closed convex hull of the original cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Polarity Correspondence

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L:=\bigl(\mathbb{R}\times\{0\}\bigr)\cup\bigl(\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}\bigr)\). assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(\bar x)=\{v:(v,-1)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mordukhovich limiting subgradients represented by normalized epigraph normals.

source_refs.locator: 2.4.1 Subgradients, Normals, and Coderivatives in Asplund Spaces p. 214
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The limiting subdifferential of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) is encoded by those limiting normals to the epigraph whose vertical component equals \(-1\): \[\partial f(\bar x)=\bigl\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:(v,-1)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\bigr\}.\] Thus normalization of a nonhorizontal epigraph normal recovers a scalar generalized gradient, while normals with zero vertical component belong instead to singular subdifferential geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A limiting subgradient is exactly the horizontal component of an epigraph normal normalized to have vertical component minus one.
knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Subgradient Encoding

children.title: Graph Tangent Geometry
children.top_down_role: Tangential structure of set-valued mapping graphs.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\) consists of all sequentially attainable first-order graph displacements.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Bouligand tangent geometry of a multifunction graph.

source_refs.locator: F. Tangent-Normal Relations p. 217
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The graph tangent cone at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is \[T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y):=\left\{(u,v):\begin{array}{l}\text{there exist }t_k\downarrow0\text{ and }(u_k,v_k)\to(u,v)\\\text{such that }\bar y+t_kv_k\in F(\bar x+t_ku_k)\text{ for every }k\end{array}\right\}.\] It records exactly the input-output velocities realizable by sequences of graph points approaching \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graph tangent cone contains precisely the input-output velocities attainable by nearby graph points at vanishing positive scales.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph Tangent Geometry

source_witnesses.locator: F. Tangent-Normal Relations p. 217
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Conic Structure of Graph Tangents
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic structure of the Bouligand tangent cone to a multifunction graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The contingent graph tangent \(T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\) is a closed cone: if \((u,v)\) is tangent and \(\lambda>0\), then \((\lambda u,\lambda v)\) is tangent. In general this cone need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graph tangent is a closed, positively homogeneous cone, but it can be nonconvex.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\) is a closed cone, not necessarily a convex cone.

notation.meaning: Bouligand tangent cone to the graph

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Conic Structure of Graph Tangents

children.title: Graph Normal Geometry
children.top_down_role: Normal structure of set-valued mapping graphs.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) has locally closed graph at \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)=\limsup_{(x,y)\to(\bar x,\bar y)}\widehat N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Mordukhovich normal geometry of a locally closed graph.

source_refs.locator: 1.1 Generalized Normals to Nonconvex Sets p. 4
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The limiting normal cone to the graph is the outer sequential limit of nearby Fréchet normal cones: \[N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y):=\left\{(x^*,y^*):\begin{array}{l}(x_k,y_k)\to(\bar x,\bar y),\ (x_k,y_k)\in\operatorname{gph}F,\\(x_k^*,y_k^*)\to(x^*,y^*),\ (x_k^*,y_k^*)\in\widehat N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(x_k,y_k)\end{array}\right\}.\] This cone is generally nonconvex and supplies the dual geometric carrier for coderivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graph normals are limits of regular normals at nearby graph points and provide the dual geometry underlying coderivatives.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph Normal Geometry

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1 Generalized Normals to Nonconvex Sets p. 4
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic structure of limiting graph normals and the tangent-polar characterization of regular graph normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=\operatorname{gph}F\) and \(\bar z=(\bar x,\bar y)\). The limiting normal cone \(N_G(\bar z)\) is a closed cone and may be nonconvex. Moreover, \[\widehat N_G(\bar z)=T_G(\bar z)^\circ\subset N_G(\bar z).\] If \(G\) is normally regular at \(\bar z\), then \[N_G(\bar z)=\widehat N_G(\bar z)=T_G(\bar z)^\circ.\] Without normal regularity the inclusion can be strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Limiting graph normals form a closed, possibly nonconvex cone; regular graph normals are the tangent polar and coincide with limiting normals under normal regularity.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) has locally closed graph at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_G(\bar z)\) is a closed cone and \(\widehat N_G(\bar z)=T_G(\bar z)^\circ\subset N_G(\bar z)\), with equality under normal regularity.

notation.meaning: regular and limiting normal cones to the graph

knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Normal Structure and Regular Polarity

children.title: Graphical Derivative Encoding
children.top_down_role: Mapping derivative information carried by graph tangents.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)=T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graphical derivative represented directly by graph tangent geometry.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Generalized Differentiation in Banach Spaces p. 3
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every direction \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define the graphical derivative by \[DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(u):=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^m:(u,v)\in T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\}.\] Equivalently, its graph is the tangent cone itself: \[\operatorname{gph}DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)=T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y).\] Hence the graphical derivative is the set-valued positively homogeneous mapping that encodes all first-order graph velocities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graphical derivative maps each input direction to the output directions paired with it in the graph tangent cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Graphical Derivative Encoding

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 1. Generalized Differentiation in Banach Spaces p. 3
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Homogeneity and Closed Graph of the Graphical Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural properties inherited from the contingent graph tangent cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The graphical derivative has a closed conic graph and is positively homogeneous: for every \(\lambda>0\), \[DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(\lambda u)=\lambda DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(u).\] Its graph and values need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graphical derivative is a closed-graph positively homogeneous multifunction, but it is generally nonconvex.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)\) is a closed, possibly nonconvex cone and \(DF(\lambda u)=\lambda DF(u)\) for \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Homogeneity and Closed Graph of the Graphical Derivative

children.title: Coderivative Encoding
children.top_down_role: Dual mapping information carried by graph normals.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) has locally closed graph at \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y)(y^*)=\{x^*:(x^*,-y^*)\in N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mordukhovich coderivative encoded by limiting normals to the graph.

source_refs.locator: 2.4.1 Subgradients, Normals, and Coderivatives in Asplund Spaces p. 214
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each covector \(y^*\in\mathbb{R}^m\), the limiting coderivative of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is \[D^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y)(y^*):=\bigl\{x^*\in\mathbb{R}^n:(x^*,-y^*)\in N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\bigr\}.\] The minus sign on the output covector fixes the standard primal-dual convention. Thus the coderivative is the multifunction obtained by slicing graph normals according to their output component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The coderivative maps an output covector to input covectors whose signed pair is a limiting normal to the graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Coderivative Encoding

source_witnesses.locator: 2.4.1 Subgradients, Normals, and Coderivatives in Asplund Spaces p. 214
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conic Homogeneity of the Limiting Coderivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic homogeneity inherited from the limiting graph-normal cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The graph of the limiting coderivative, \[\operatorname{gph}D^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=\{(y^*,x^*):(x^*,-y^*)\in N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\},\] is a closed cone. Consequently, for every \(\lambda>0\), \[D^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y)(\lambda y^*)=\lambda D^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y)(y^*).\] Its graph and values need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting coderivative has a closed conic graph and is positively homogeneous, but it is generally nonconvex.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) has locally closed graph at \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}D^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\) is a closed, possibly nonconvex cone and \(D^*F(\lambda y^*)=\lambda D^*F(y^*)\) for \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Conic Homogeneity of the Limiting Coderivative

children.title: Horizontal Epigraph Geometry
children.top_down_role: Horizontal directions governing recession-like local behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)=\{v:(v,0)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Horizontal epigraph normals encode the singular subdifferential.

source_refs.locator: 2.4.2 Representations of Singular Subgradients and Horizontal Normals to Graphs and Epigraphs p. 223
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vector \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is a singular subgradient of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) exactly when it is the horizontal component of a limiting epigraph normal having zero vertical component: \[\partial^\infty f(\bar x)=\bigl\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:(v,0)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\bigr\}.\] These horizontal normals cannot be normalized to vertical component \(-1\), so they record recession-type first-order behavior rather than ordinary limiting subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Horizontal limiting normals to the epigraph, identified by zero vertical component, are exactly the singular subgradients.
knowledge_statements.title: Horizontal Epigraph Geometry

source_witnesses.locator: 2.4.2 Representations of Singular Subgradients and Horizontal Normals to Graphs and Epigraphs p. 223
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed decomposition is broader than this horizontal-slice leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every \((v,\alpha)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\) satisfies \(\alpha\le0\); negative-height normals rescale to ordinary subgradients, while zero-height normals represent singular subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epigraph normals decompose into negative-height ordinary-subgradient normals and horizontal singular normals.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\operatorname{epi}f}=\{\lambda(u,-1):\lambda>0,u\in\partial f\}\cup(\partial^\infty f\times\{0\})\) at the graph point.
knowledge_statements.title: Vertical-Slice Decomposition of Epigraph Normals

children.title: Singular Normal Geometry
children.top_down_role: Dual horizontal structure associated with non-Lipschitz behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\in\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\iff(v,0)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singular subgradients defined through zero-height limiting epigraph normals.

source_refs.locator: 2.4.2 Representations of Singular Subgradients and Horizontal Normals to Graphs and Epigraphs p. 223
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The singular normal geometry of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) is the cone \[\partial^\infty f(\bar x):=\bigl\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:(v,0)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\bigr\}.\] Equivalently, its elements are limits \(v_k\to v\) of scaled regular subgradients \(v_k=\lambda_k u_k\), where \(x_k\to\bar x\), \(f(x_k)\to f(\bar x)\), \(u_k\in\widehat\partial f(x_k)\), and \(\lambda_k\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Singular subgradients are horizontal epigraph normals, equivalently limits of regular subgradients scaled by positive factors tending to zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular Normal Geometry

source_witnesses.locator: 2.4.2 Representations of Singular Subgradients and Horizontal Normals to Graphs and Epigraphs p. 223
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Conic Structure of the Singular Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic algebraic structure of the singular subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The singular subdifferential \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\) is a closed cone containing the origin: \(0\in\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\) and \(\lambda\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\subset\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\) for every \(\lambda\ge0\). It need not be convex for a general lower-semicontinuous nonconvex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The singular subdifferential is a closed cone containing zero but need not be convex.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\) is a closed cone, not necessarily convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Conic Structure of the Singular Subdifferential

children.title: Non-Lipschitz Regimes
children.top_down_role: Function regimes exhibiting nontrivial horizontal geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\ne\{0\}\) rules out local Lipschitz continuity of \(f\) around \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonzero singular subgradients detect failure of local Lipschitz regularity.

source_refs.locator: 2.4.2 Representations of Singular Subgradients and Horizontal Normals to Graphs and Epigraphs p. 223
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is finite and locally Lipschitz on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\), then its singular subdifferential is trivial: \[\partial^\infty f(\bar x)=\{0\}.\] Therefore, the existence of \(v\ne0\) with \((v,0)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\) certifies that \(f\) is not locally Lipschitz around \(\bar x\). The converse need not hold without additional regularity, so trivial singular geometry alone does not universally establish Lipschitz continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every locally Lipschitz function has only the zero singular subgradient; a nonzero one therefore certifies non-Lipschitz behavior.
knowledge_statements.title: Non-Lipschitz Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 2.4.2 Representations of Singular Subgradients and Horizontal Normals to Graphs and Epigraphs p. 223
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.title: Horizontal Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Loss of stable finite-slope behavior through horizontal directions.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\cap(\mathbb{R}^n\times\{0\})\ne\{(0,0)\}\) is horizontal degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy means existence of a nonzero horizontal limiting epigraph normal.

source_refs.locator: 2.4.2 Representations of Singular Subgradients and Horizontal Normals to Graphs and Epigraphs p. 223
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The epigraph is horizontally degenerate at \((\bar x,f(\bar x))\) when \[N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\cap\bigl(\mathbb{R}^n\times\{0\}\bigr)\ne\{(0,0)\}.\] By singular-normal encoding, this condition is equivalent to \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\ne\{0\}\). Such a normal has no nonzero vertical component and therefore cannot be rescaled into the form \((v,-1)\) used to encode ordinary limiting subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Horizontal degeneracy occurs exactly when the epigraph has a nonzero limiting normal with zero vertical component.
knowledge_statements.title: Horizontal Degeneracy

source_witnesses.locator: 2.4.2 Representations of Singular Subgradients and Horizontal Normals to Graphs and Epigraphs p. 223
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent sequence test for the degeneracy condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Horizontal degeneracy at \(\bar x\) is equivalent to the existence of \(x_k\to\bar x\), \(f(x_k)\to f(\bar x)\), \(u_k\in\widehat\partial f(x_k)\), and \(\lambda_k\downarrow0\) such that \(\lambda_k u_k\to v\ne0\). Necessarily \(\|u_k\|\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Horizontal degeneracy is witnessed by a nonzero limit of vanishing rescalings of nearby regular subgradients; those subgradients must be unbounded.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\ne\{0\}\iff\exists x_k,u_k,\lambda_k:\lambda_k u_k\to v\ne0\), with \(\|u_k\|\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Criterion for Horizontal Degeneracy

children.title: Distance-Function Subdifferentiation
children.top_down_role: Normal-cone representations obtained through distance functions.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and closed.
\(\bar x\in C\), and \(d_C(x):=\inf_{z\in C}\|x-z\|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial d_C(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x)\cap\mathbb{B}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional limiting subdifferentiation of distance at points of the set.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.3 Subdifferentiation of Distance Functions p. 97
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At every point \(\bar x\in C\), the limiting subdifferential of the distance function is the unit truncation of the limiting normal cone: \[\partial d_C(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x)\cap\mathbb{B}.\] Equivalently, the full normal cone is recovered by positive scaling, \[N_C(\bar x)=\bigcup_{\lambda\ge0}\lambda\,\partial d_C(\bar x).\] Thus distance-function subgradients encode exactly the limiting normal directions whose norm does not exceed one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point of a closed set, distance subgradients are exactly the limiting normals of norm at most one.
knowledge_statements.title: Distance-Function Subdifferentiation

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3.3 Subdifferentiation of Distance Functions p. 97

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz and Horizon Properties of the Distance Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global first-order bounds for distance functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The distance function is globally one-Lipschitz: \(|d_C(x)-d_C(y)|\le\|x-y\|\). Consequently, \(\partial d_C(x)\subset\mathbb B\) and \(\partial^\infty d_C(x)=\{0\}\) for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to a nonempty closed set is one-Lipschitz, has subgradients of norm at most one, and has trivial horizon subdifferential.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lip}(d_C)\le1\), \(\partial d_C(x)\subset\mathbb B\), and \(\partial^\infty d_C(x)=\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: horizon subdifferential of the distance function

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At every \(\bar x\in C\), \(\widehat\partial d_C(\bar x)=\widehat N_C(\bar x)\cap\mathbb B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point of the set, regular distance subgradients are exactly regular normals of norm at most one.

\(\bar x\in C\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exterior representation through nearest points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x\notin C\) and \(v\in\partial d_C(x)\), then \(\|v\|=1\) and there exists \(p\in P_C(x)\) such that \(v=(x-p)/d_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every limiting distance subgradient outside a closed finite-dimensional set is a unit displacement from a nearest point toward the query point.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and closed.
\(x\notin C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\in\partial d_C(x)\Rightarrow\exists p\in P_C(x):v=(x-p)/d_C(x),\ \|v\|=1\).

knowledge_statements.title: Distance Subgradients Outside the Set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-convex specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\) is closed and convex, then \[\partial d_C(x)=\begin{cases}N_C(x)\cap\mathbb B,&x\in C,\\ \left\{\dfrac{x-P_Cx}{d_C(x)}\right\},&x\notin C.\end{cases}\] Thus \(d_C\) is differentiable off \(C\), with \(\nabla d_C(x)=(x-P_Cx)/d_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex set, the distance subdifferential is the truncated normal cone on the set and the normalized projection residual off the set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial d_C(x)=N_C(x)\cap\mathbb B\) on \(C\), and \(\partial d_C(x)=\{(x-P_Cx)/d_C(x)\}\) off \(C\).

notation.meaning: unique Euclidean projection of x onto C

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vector \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is a proximal normal to \(C\) at \(\bar x\) precisely when some point displaced from \(\bar x\) along \(v\) projects back to \(\bar x\): \[v\in N_C^P(\bar x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists r>0\text{ such that }\bar x\in P_C(\bar x+rv).\] Equivalently, for some \(\sigma\ge0\), \[\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle\le\sigma\|x-\bar x\|^2\quad\text{for all }x\in C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal normal points from a set point toward an exterior point for which that set point is nearest.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(C\) is closed, and its distance and metric projection at the origin satisfy \[d_C(0)=1\quad\text{and}\quad P_C(0)=\varnothing.\] Thus the finite distance from \(0\) to this closed subset of \(H\) is not attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The displayed closed subset of an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space has finite distance one from the origin but contains no nearest point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Names the set property whose failure is exhibited by the seed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty set \(C\) in a metric space is proximinal if \(P_C(x):=\{c\in C:d(x,c)=d_C(x)\}\ne\varnothing\) for every \(x\). Distance nonattainment at \(x\) is precisely \(P_C(x)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is proximinal when every query point has a nearest point; nonattainment means the projection set is empty at a query.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty subset of a metric space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ proximinal}\iff P_C(x)\ne\varnothing\ \forall x\); nonattainment at \(x\iff P_C(x)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Proximinality and Distance Attainment

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Convex Hilbert Sets Attain Distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary showing that infinite dimensionality alone does not cause nonattainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every nonempty closed convex subset \(C\) of a Hilbert space has a unique nearest point to each \(x\); equivalently, \(P_C(x)\) is a singleton for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed convex Hilbert-space sets always have unique nearest points.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space.
\(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|P_C(x)|=1\) for every \(x\in H\).
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex Hilbert Sets Attain Distance

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Excludes closed-set nonattainment in Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every nonempty closed subset \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is proximinal: \(P_C(x)\ne\varnothing\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty closed Euclidean set has a nearest point.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_C(x)\ne\varnothing\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Attainment Boundary

children.title: Projection Nonuniqueness
children.top_down_role: Geometries admitting multiple nearest-point selections.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Points at which an attained metric projection has multiple values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty set \(C\) in a metric space, define \[\mathcal M(C):=\{x:|P_C(x)|\ge2\},\qquad P_C(x):=\{c\in C:d(x,c)=d_C(x)\}.\] Thus projection nonuniqueness at \(x\) means \(x\in\mathcal M(C)\); it is distinct from nonattainment, where \(P_C(x)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonunique-projection locus consists of points having at least two nearest points; nonattainment is a different pathology.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty subset of a metric space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\mathcal M(C)\iff |P_C(x)|\ge2\), while nonattainment means \(P_C(x)=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: set of nearest points in C to x

knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique-Projection Locus

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural regime in which the local failure cannot occur.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space \(H\), then \(P_C(x)\) is a singleton for every \(x\in H\). Closedness alone does not ensure uniqueness, as the immutable two-point example demonstrates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed convex subsets of Hilbert space have unique projections, while closed nonconvex sets may have several nearest points.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space.
\(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall x\in H,\ |P_C(x)|=1\).
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Excludes Hilbert-Space Projection Nonuniqueness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonconvex closed sets may have several nearest points even in one dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the closed nonconvex set \(C=\{-1,1\}\), the distance and metric projection at the origin are \[d_C(0)=1\quad\text{and}\quad P_C(0)=\{-1,1\}.\] Hence the metric projection is not single-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The origin has two nearest points in the closed nonconvex set consisting of minus one and one.

children.title: Projection Instability
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of nearest-point selections to perturbations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radial Projection Instability for the Unit Circle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A distinct self-contained example of failure of every continuous local nearest-point selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{u\in\mathbb R^2:\|u\|=1\}\). Then \(P_C(0)=C\), whereas for every \(z\ne0\) with \(\|z\|<1\), \(P_C(z)=\{z/\|z\|\}\). Hence no single-valued selection of \(P_C\) defined on a neighborhood of \(0\) is continuous at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto the unit circle is forced to follow the radial direction away from the center, so no nearest-point selection can be continuous at the center.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_C(0)=C\), \(P_C(z)=\{z/\|z\|\}\) for \(0<\|z\|<1\), and no local single-valued selection is continuous at \(0\).

notation.meaning: metric projection set onto the unit circle

knowledge_statements.title: Radial Projection Instability for the Unit Circle

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No single-valued selection of \(P_C\) defined on a neighborhood of \(z_0\) is continuous at \(z_0\).

notation.meaning: Metric projection set onto the two-point set

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection selections can jump at points where nearest points bifurcate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Along \(z_s=(s,0)\), the metric projection satisfies \[P_C(z_s)=\begin{cases}\{(-1,0)\},&-1<s<0,\\ \{(-1,0),(1,0)\},&s=0,\\ \{(1,0)\},&0<s<1.\end{cases}\] Consequently, no single-valued selection of \(P_C\) defined on a neighborhood of \(z_0\) is continuous at \(z_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the projection tie at the origin, arbitrarily small perturbations switch the unique nearest point between two separated values, so no local single-valued projection selection is continuous there.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Instability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound theorem, but primarily owned by convex projection geometry rather than this pathology leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty closed convex set \(C\) in a Hilbert space, \(P_C\) is single-valued and firmly nonexpansive: \(\|P_Cx-P_Cy\|^2\le\langle P_Cx-P_Cy,x-y\rangle\). Consequently, \(P_C\) is one-Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a nonempty closed convex Hilbert-space set is firmly nonexpansive and one-Lipschitz.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space.
\(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_C\) is firmly nonexpansive and therefore \(1\)-Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.title: Firm Stability of Convex Projections

children.title: Normal-Recovery Failure
children.top_down_role: Breakdown of normal representations derived from projection behavior.

assumptions_latex: The projection construction associates \(y-p\) with a proximal normal to \(C\) at \(p\) when \(p\in P_C(y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Because \(P_C(y)=\varnothing\), this projection-based construction cannot produce a proximal normal to \(C\) from the query point \(y\).

notation.meaning: Projection-generated proximal-normal displacement at a projected point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of distance attainment blocks the projection construction of proximal normals; it does not assert that the set has no proximal normals at its own points.

children.top_down_role: Upper, lower, and one-sided Dini derivative regimes.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space, \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), and \(f(x)\in\mathbb R\).
\(h\in X\).

source_refs.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The lower and upper one-sided Dini directional derivatives of \(f\) at \(x\) in direction \(h\) are, respectively, \[f'_-(x;h)=\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+th)-f(x)}{t},\qquad f'_+(x;h)=\limsup_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+th)-f(x)}{t}.\] Their values lie in \(\overline{\mathbb R}\). If the two values coincide, their common value is the one-sided Dini directional derivative \(f'(x;h)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dini derivatives measure lower and upper first-order growth while the direction remains fixed and the step approaches zero from above.
knowledge_statements.title: Dini Directional Derivatives

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159
source_witnesses.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Core structure of fixed-direction lower and upper Dini derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\lambda>0\), \(f'_{\pm}(x;\lambda h)=\lambda f'_{\pm}(x;h)\). If \(d_H^-f\) and \(d_H^+f\) denote the lower and upper perturbed-direction limits, then \[d_H^-f(x;h)\le f'_-(x;h)\le f'_+(x;h)\le d_H^+f(x;h).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dini derivatives are positively homogeneous; allowing directional perturbations lowers the lower limit and raises the upper limit.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space, \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), and \(f(x)\in\mathbb R\).
\(h\in X\) and \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'_{\pm}(x;\lambda h)=\lambda f'_{\pm}(x;h)\) and \(d_H^-f(x;h)\le f'_-(x;h)\le f'_+(x;h)\le d_H^+f(x;h)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Homogeneity and Hadamard–Dini Ordering

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower Dini derivatives are nonnegative at a local minimum.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is a local minimizer of \(f\) and \(f(x)\) is finite.

children.title: Hadamard Directional Derivatives
children.top_down_role: Directional derivatives stable under perturbation of directions.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are normed spaces, \(F:X\to Y\), and \(x,h\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F'_H(x;h)\) exists when all quotients with \(t\downarrow0\) and perturbed directions \(h'\to h\) have one common limit in \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided directional differentiation robust to perturbations of the direction.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159
source_refs.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Hadamard directional derivative of \(F\) at \(x\) in direction \(h\) is the vector \(F'_H(x;h)\in Y\), when it exists, satisfying \[F'_H(x;h)=\lim_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\h'\to h}}\frac{F(x+t h')-F(x)}{t}.\] Equivalently, the quotient converges to the same value for every pair of sequences \(t_k\downarrow0\) and \(h_k\to h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hadamard directional derivative has one common value when the positive step tends to zero and the direction is allowed to approach the specified direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Hadamard Directional Derivatives

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159
source_witnesses.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural property of the perturbed-direction limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F'_H(x;h)\) exists, then for every \(\lambda>0\), \[F'_H(x;\lambda h)=\lambda F'_H(x;h).\] If the derivative exists at \(h=0\), its value is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hadamard directional derivatives scale positively with the direction.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\to Y\), \(F'_H(x;h)\) exists, and \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F'_H(x;\lambda h)=\lambda F'_H(x;h)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Scaling of Hadamard Directional Derivatives

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Lipschitz Criterion for Hadamard Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient condition upgrading a fixed-direction limit to a perturbed-direction limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F\) is locally Lipschitz near \(x\) and \(\lim_{t\downarrow0}[F(x+th)-F(x)]/t=L\), then \[F'_H(x;h)=L.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a locally Lipschitz mapping, an existing ordinary directional derivative is Hadamard stable.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are normed spaces and \(F:X\to Y\) is locally Lipschitz near \(x\).
The ordinary one-sided directional derivative in direction \(h\) exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F'_H(x;h)=\lim_{t\downarrow0}[F(x+th)-F(x)]/t\).
knowledge_statements.title: Local Lipschitz Criterion for Hadamard Stability

notation.meaning: Bouligand derivative model at the base point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bouligand differentiability as a positively homogeneous first-order expansion.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159
source_refs.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is Bouligand differentiable at \(x\) if there exists a continuous positively homogeneous mapping \(F'_B(x;\cdot):X\to Y\) such that \[F(x+u)=F(x)+F'_B(x;u)+r(u),\qquad \lim_{\substack{u\to0\\u\ne0}}\frac{\|r(u)\|}{\|u\|}=0.\] Positive homogeneity means \(F'_B(x;\lambda h)=\lambda F'_B(x;h)\) for every \(h\in X\) and \(\lambda\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bouligand differentiability supplies a continuous positively homogeneous first-order model whose approximation error is smaller than the increment norm.
knowledge_statements.title: Bouligand Directional Differentiability

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159
source_witnesses.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\to Y\) is Bouligand differentiable at \(x\).
\(G:Y\to Z\) is Bouligand differentiable at \(F(x)\).
\(X,Y,Z\) are normed spaces.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact first-order chain rule for composable Bouligand-differentiable mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F\) is Bouligand differentiable at \(x\) and \(G\) is Bouligand differentiable at \(F(x)\), then \(G\circ F\) is Bouligand differentiable at \(x\), with \[(G\circ F)'_B(x;h)=G'_B\bigl(F(x);F'_B(x;h)\bigr)\qquad(h\in X).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bouligand derivatives obey the ordinary composition rule, with the outer positively homogeneous model applied to the inner model.
knowledge_statements.title: Bouligand Chain Rule

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional normed spaces.
\(F:X\to Y\) and \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bouligand differentiability is equivalent to a continuous positively homogeneous map giving all perturbed-direction quotient limits, and that map is unique.
review_flags: Finite dimensionality is essential to the stated equivalence from pointwise perturbed-direction limits to the uniform little-o expansion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional equivalence between the uniform Bouligand expansion and a continuous all-direction Hadamard derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is Bouligand differentiable at \(x\) if and only if there exists a continuous positively homogeneous mapping \(A:X\to Y\) such that, for every \(h\in X\), every \(t_k\downarrow0\), and every \(h_k\to h\), \[\frac{F(x+t_kh_k)-F(x)}{t_k}\to A(h).\] In that case \(A\) is unique, \(A(h)=F'_B(x;h)=F'(x;h)\), and \[F(x+u)-F(x)-A(u)=o(\|u\|).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, Bouligand differentiability is equivalent to possessing one continuous positively homogeneous Hadamard derivative model in every direction; that model is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hadamard Characterization of the Bouligand Model
knowledge_statements.title: Hadamard Characterization of the Bouligand Model

children.title: Clarke Generalized Directional Derivative
children.top_down_role: Robust directional growth for locally Lipschitz functions.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space and \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz near \(x\).
\(h\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{\circ}(x;h)=\limsup_{y\to x,\,t\downarrow0}[f(y+th)-f(y)]/t\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarke's robust upper directional growth for locally Lipschitz real-valued functions.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159
source_refs.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Clarke generalized directional derivative of \(f\) at \(x\) in direction \(h\) is \[f^{\circ}(x;h)=\limsup_{\substack{y\to x\\t\downarrow0}}\frac{f(y+th)-f(y)}{t}.\] The base point may vary with the step, making this derivative robust under nearby perturbations. Local Lipschitz continuity ensures that \(f^{\circ}(x;h)\) is finite for every \(h\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke derivative takes the worst limiting directional growth over positive steps and nearby base points.
knowledge_statements.title: Clarke Generalized Directional Derivative

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Moving-Base Strictness for a Concave Corner
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Example separating robust nearby-base growth from fixed-base directional growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(u)=-|u|\), \[f'(0;h)=-|h|,\qquad f^{\circ}(0;h)=|h|.\] Thus the Clarke derivative strictly exceeds the fixed-base derivative whenever \(h\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a concave absolute-value corner, fixed-base growth is negative while robust nearby-base growth is positive.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \(f(u)=-|u|\).
knowledge_statements.title: Moving-Base Strictness for a Concave Corner

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical coincidence regimes for robust upper directional growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is continuously Fréchet differentiable near \(x\), then \(f^{\circ}(x;h)=\langle\nabla f(x),h\rangle\). If \(f\) is convex and locally Lipschitz near \(x\), then \(f^{\circ}(x;h)=f'(x;h)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke derivative reduces to the gradient pairing for smooth functions and to the ordinary directional derivative for locally Lipschitz convex functions.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is either continuously Fréchet differentiable near \(x\), or convex and locally Lipschitz near \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{\circ}(x;h)=\langle\nabla f(x),h\rangle\) in the smooth case and \(f^{\circ}(x;h)=f'(x;h)\) in the convex case.
knowledge_statements.title: Smooth and Convex Specializations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Core directional structure under local Lipschitz continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is Lipschitz with constant \(L\) near \(x\), then \(h\mapsto f^{\circ}(x;h)\) is positively homogeneous and subadditive, and \[|f^{\circ}(x;h)|\le L\|h\|.\] Hence it is finite, continuous, and sublinear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke derivative is a finite continuous sublinear function bounded by the local Lipschitz constant.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is Lipschitz with constant \(L\) near \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{\circ}(x;\lambda h)=\lambda f^{\circ}(x;h)\), \(f^{\circ}(x;h+k)\le f^{\circ}(x;h)+f^{\circ}(x;k)\), and \(|f^{\circ}(x;h)|\le L\|h\|\).
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Sublinear Directional Model

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional normed space, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) satisfy \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb R\), and fix \(h\in X\). assumptions_latex: \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb R\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict separation of the lower and upper values is exactly failure of the perturbed-direction quotient to have an extended-real limit; when both endpoints are finite their difference is a positive scalar gap.
review_flags: This corrects the deferred seed by distinguishing scalar quotient nonconvergence from failure or nonuniqueness of an epigraphical set limit.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of one perturbed-direction first-order limit through strict lower-upper separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[q_t(h'):=\frac{f(\bar x+th')-f(\bar x)}{t},\] one always has \(d^-f(\bar x;h)\le d^+f(\bar x;h)\). If both endpoints are finite, define \[G(\bar x;h):=d^+f(\bar x;h)-d^-f(\bar x;h).\] Then \(G(\bar x;h)>0\) if and only if \(q_t(h')\) has no limit as \(t\downarrow0\) and \(h'\to h\). More generally, unequal extended-real endpoints imply the same nonconvergence, but no numerical gap is defined when extended-real subtraction is indeterminate. This conclusion concerns the scalar joint limit and does not by itself assert failure or nonuniqueness of a Painleve-Kuratowski epigraphical limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Different lower and upper perturbed-direction values prevent a single first-order quotient limit; a numerical gap is used only when both endpoints are finite.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is properly epi-differentiable at \(\bar x\) if there exists a proper lower-semicontinuous function \(d_e f(\bar x):X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) such that \[q_t\xrightarrow{e}d_e f(\bar x)\quad\text{as }t\downarrow0.\] Equivalently, \(\operatorname{epi}q_t\) converges to \(\operatorname{epi}d_e f(\bar x)\) in the Painleve-Kuratowski sense. The limit is unique and is the proper first epi-derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proper epi-differentiability means that the first-order difference quotients epi-converge to one proper lower-semicontinuous function.
knowledge_statements.title: Proper First Epi-Differentiability

assumptions_latex: The assumptions and notation of proper first epi-differentiability hold.
Convergence is interpreted sequentially in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_t\xrightarrow{e}g\) exactly when every vanishing-scale convergent-direction sequence satisfies the liminf inequality and every direction has recovery directions along every vanishing scale sequence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential characterization and failure boundary for the first-order quotient family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper lower-semicontinuous \(g\), the convergence \(q_t\xrightarrow{e}g\) as \(t\downarrow0\) is equivalent to both conditions: (i) for every \(t_k\downarrow0\) and \(h_k\to h\), \[\liminf_{k\to\infty}q_{t_k}(h_k)\ge g(h);\] and (ii) for every \(h\) and every \(t_k\downarrow0\), there exist \(h_k\to h\) such that \[\limsup_{k\to\infty}q_{t_k}(h_k)\le g(h).\] Thus proper epi-differentiability fails exactly when no single proper lower-semicontinuous \(g\) satisfies both requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epi-differentiability is characterized by a universal lower-limit inequality and recovery directions along every vanishing sequence of scales.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Epi-Differentiability Test

knowledge_statements.title: Directionally Regular Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarke directional regularity for finite-valued locally Lipschitz functions on finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional normed space and let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\). Suppose that for every \(h\in X\) the directional derivative \[f'(\bar x;h):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(\bar x+th)-f(\bar x)}{t}\] exists. Define the Clarke generalized directional derivative by \[f^{\circ}(\bar x;h):=\limsup_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\t\downarrow0}}\frac{f(x+th)-f(x)}{t}.\] The function \(f\) is directionally regular at \(\bar x\) if \[f'(\bar x;h)=f^{\circ}(\bar x;h)\quad\text{for every }h\in X.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz function is directionally regular at a point when each ordinary directional derivative exists and equals the corresponding Clarke generalized directional derivative.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed space.
\(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
\(f'(\bar x;h)\) exists for every \(h\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is directionally regular at \(\bar x\) when \(f'(\bar x;h)=f^{\circ}(\bar x;h)\) for every \(h\in X\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp counterexample showing that local Lipschitz continuity and existence of all directional derivatives do not imply directional regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=-|x|\), the ordinary directional derivative exists in every direction and equals \[f'(0;h)=-|h|.\] The Clarke generalized directional derivative is \[f^\circ(0;h)=|h|.\] Thus the two derivatives disagree for every \(h\ne0\), and \(f\) is not directionally regular at zero. Equivalently, the ordinary directional derivative is not sublinear and therefore cannot be a support function. This also shows that negation need not preserve directional regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The locally Lipschitz function minus absolute value has all ordinary directional derivatives, but they equal minus absolute value rather than the Clarke derivative absolute value.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional Differentiability Does Not Imply Regularity

notation.meaning: Convex subdifferential, equal here to the Clarke subdifferential

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical smooth and convex regimes in which ordinary and Clarke directional constructions coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\), then \[f'(\bar x;h)=f^\circ(\bar x;h)=\langle\nabla f(\bar x),h\rangle.\] If \(f\) is convex and locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\), then \[f'(\bar x;h)=f^\circ(\bar x;h)=\max_{v\in\partial f(\bar x)}\langle v,h\rangle.\] Hence both classes are directionally regular at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuously differentiable functions and locally Lipschitz convex functions are directionally regular, with gradient and subgradient support formulas respectively.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Smooth and Convex Regimes

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional.
\(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) and directionally regular at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(\bar x;h)=\sigma_{\partial^C f(\bar x)}(h)=\max_{v\in\partial^C f(\bar x)}\langle v,h\rangle\) for every \(h\), and \(h\mapsto f'(\bar x;h)\) is finite, continuous, and sublinear.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent dual representation and immediate structural consequences of Clarke directional regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite-valued locally Lipschitz function on a finite-dimensional space, \(f^\circ(\bar x;h)=\max_{v\in\partial^C f(\bar x)}\langle v,h\rangle\). Consequently, \(f\) is directionally regular at \(\bar x\) if and only if its ordinary directional derivative exists in every direction and satisfies \[f'(\bar x;h)=\max_{v\in\partial^C f(\bar x)}\langle v,h\rangle\quad\text{for all }h.\] In that case \(h\mapsto f'(\bar x;h)\) is a finite continuous sublinear function. In particular, an existing directional derivative that is not sublinear cannot be directionally regular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a directionally regular point, the ordinary directional derivative is exactly the support function of the Clarke subdifferential and is therefore continuous and sublinear.
knowledge_statements.title: Clarke-Subdifferential Support Representation

assumptions_latex: \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:X\to\mathbb R\) are locally Lipschitz and directionally regular at \(\bar x\).
\(\lambda_i\ge0\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_i\lambda_i f_i\) and \(\max_i f_i\) are directionally regular at \(\bar x\), with the stated derivative formulas.

notation.meaning: Indices attaining the finite maximum at the base point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary closure calculus for Clarke-directionally regular locally Lipschitz functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\) be locally Lipschitz and directionally regular at \(\bar x\). For coefficients \(\lambda_i\ge0\), the function \(g=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i\) is directionally regular and \[g'(\bar x;h)=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i'(\bar x;h).\] The finite maximum \(F=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i\) is also directionally regular and \[F'(\bar x;h)=\max_{i\in I(\bar x)}f_i'(\bar x;h),\qquad I(\bar x)=\{i:f_i(\bar x)=F(\bar x)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative finite sums and finite maxima preserve directional regularity, with sum and active-index maximum derivative formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure Under Nonnegative Sums and Finite Maxima

children.title: Piecewise-Smooth Directional Models

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Smooth Directional Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite continuous selections of smooth functions and their branchwise first-order models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subset\mathbb R^n\) be open. A continuous function \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) is piecewise smooth if there are finitely many functions \(\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_m\in C^1(U)\) such that \[f(x)\in\{\phi_1(x),\ldots,\phi_m(x)\}\quad\text{for every }x\in U.\] Define \[I(x):=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:f(x)=\phi_i(x)\}.\] If \(i\in I(\bar x)\), \(t_k\downarrow0\), \(h_k\to h\), and \(f(\bar x+t_kh_k)=\phi_i(\bar x+t_kh_k)\), then \[\frac{f(\bar x+t_kh_k)-f(\bar x)}{t_k}\to\nabla\phi_i(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}h.\] Thus branchwise first-order limits are drawn from finitely many linear models.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise-smooth function selects among finitely many smooth pieces; along a sequence that remains on one active piece, its first-order quotient converges to that piece's linearization.
assumptions_latex: \(U\subset\mathbb R^n\) is open and \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) is continuous.
\(\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_m\in C^1(U)\) are finitely many selections satisfying \(f(x)\in\{\phi_1(x),\ldots,\phi_m(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If a sequence approaching \(\bar x\) in direction \(h\) remains on an active branch \(i\), its first-order quotient converges to \(\nabla\phi_i(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}h\).

notation.meaning: indices of smooth pieces agreeing with f at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order regularity forced by a finite continuous piecewise-C1 scalar selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) be a continuous selection of finitely many \(C^1\) functions \(\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_m\). Then \(f\) is locally Lipschitz and Bouligand differentiable at every \(\bar x\in U\). Its derivative \(f'_B(\bar x;\cdot)\) is continuous, positively homogeneous, and piecewise linear, and \[f'_B(\bar x;h)\in\{\nabla\phi_i(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}h:i\in I(\bar x)\}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^n).\] Moreover, \[f(\bar x+u)=f(\bar x)+f'_B(\bar x;u)+o(\|u\|).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite continuous piecewise-C1 scalar selection is locally Lipschitz and Bouligand differentiable, with a continuous piecewise-linear derivative selected from active branch linearizations.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Selection Bouligand Regularity

knowledge_statements.title: Directional Limit Nonexistence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous one-dimensional counterexample to existence of a one-sided directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) by \[f(0)=0,\qquad f(x)=x\sin(\log(1/|x|))\quad(x\ne0).\] The function is continuous at \(0\), while its directional quotient in direction \(1\) satisfies \[\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(t)-f(0)}{t}=-1<1=\limsup_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(t)-f(0)}{t}.\] Therefore \(f'(0;1)\) does not exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This continuous oscillatory function has directional quotients with lower limit −1 and upper limit 1, so its directional derivative at zero in direction one does not exist.

knowledge_statements.title: Directional Limit Oscillation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistent bounded oscillation separating lower and upper directional limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) by \[f(0)=0,\qquad f(x)=x\sin(1/x)\quad(x\ne0).\] Its fixed-direction quotient satisfies \[\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(t)-f(0)}{t}=-1<1=\limsup_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(t)-f(0)}{t}.\] Under the perturbed-direction Hadamard convention, the same endpoint values hold at direction \(1\): \[d^-f(0;1)=-1<1=d^+f(0;1).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For this function the quotient oscillates persistently between −1 and 1; both the fixed-direction and perturbed-direction lower and upper limits remain separated.

knowledge_statements.title: Base-Point Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vanishing directional derivatives at one point with unbounded classical derivatives at nearby base points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) by \[f(0)=0,\qquad f(x)=x^2\sin(1/x^2)\quad(x\ne0).\] Then \[f'(0;h)=0\quad\text{for every }h\in\mathbb R,\] whereas for \(x\ne0\), \[f'(x)=2x\sin(1/x^2)-\frac{2}{x}\cos(1/x^2),\] and \(f'\) is unbounded on every neighborhood of \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every directional derivative at zero vanishes, but the classical derivatives at nearby nonzero points are unbounded.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(x)=x^2\sin(1/x^2)\) for \(x\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(0;h)=0\) for every \(h\in\mathbb R\), but \(f'\) is unbounded on every neighborhood of \(0\).

knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Model Breakdown
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hölder growth below order one prevents a finite directional model at linear scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be given by \(f(x)=|x|^{1/2}\). For every \(h\ne0\), \[\frac{f(th)-f(0)}{t}=|h|^{1/2}t^{-1/2}\to+\infty\quad\text{as }t\downarrow0.\] Thus no finite-valued first-order directional model at scale \(t\) represents the nonzero directions at the origin.
