knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous two-dimensional example separating existence of all fixed-ray directional derivatives from a uniform first-order approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[f(0,0)=0,\qquad f(x,y)=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\,\frac{x^3y}{x^6+y^2}\quad ((x,y)\ne(0,0)).\] The fraction has absolute value at most \(1/2\), so \(f\) is continuous at the origin. For every fixed \(h\in\mathbb R^2\), \(f'(0;h)=0\). Nevertheless, along \(z_s=(s,s^3)\), \[\frac{f(z_s)-f(0)-f'(0;z_s)}{\|z_s\|}=\frac12\] for every \(s\ne0\). Thus the pointwise directional derivative exists in every direction but does not give a uniform first-order approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All fixed-ray directional derivatives at the origin are zero, yet along a curved approach the normalized error remains one half, so the zero directional model is not a uniform first-order model.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a proper convex function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), the convex subdifferential is
\[
\partial f(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid f(x)\ge f(\bar x)+\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle\ \text{for all }x\in\mathbb{R}^n\right\}.
\]
Thus \(v\) is a convex subgradient exactly when the affine function with slope \(v\) passing through \((\bar x,f(\bar x))\) globally minorizes \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex subgradient is the slope of an affine function supporting the graph from below at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Subdifferential

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(v\in\mathbb R^n\), \[v\in\partial f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(x)+f^*(v)=\langle v,x\rangle\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in\partial f^*(v).\] Hence \((\partial f)^{-1}=\partial f^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex subgradient membership is equality in Fenchel-Young, and conjugacy reverses the subdifferential relation.

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\Rightarrow\partial f(x)\ne\varnothing\); if \(f\) is finite near \(x\), differentiability at \(x\) is equivalent to \(\partial f(x)\) being a singleton.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise finite-dimensional structure of a proper convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\), \(\partial f(x)\) is closed and convex, and it is nonempty when \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\). If \(f\) is finite on a neighborhood of \(x\), then \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\) if and only if \(\partial f(x)\) is a singleton, in which case \(\partial f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\}\). At boundary points of the domain the subdifferential can be empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex subgradients exist throughout the relative interior, and a singleton subdifferential characterizes differentiability at locally finite points.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonemptiness and Differentiability Tests

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) finite at \(\bar x\), the proximal subdifferential is
\[
\partial_P f(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid \exists r>0,\ \exists\delta>0:\ f(x)\ge f(\bar x)+\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle-\frac r2\|x-\bar x\|^2\ \text{whenever }\|x-\bar x\|<\delta\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(v\in\partial_P f(\bar x)\) when \(\bar x\) is a local minimizer of \(x\mapsto f(x)-\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle+(r/2)\|x-\bar x\|^2\) for some \(r>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal subgradient supplies a local affine lower support after allowing a negative quadratic error.
knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Subdifferential

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) finite at \(\bar x\), its Fréchet subdifferential is
\[
\widehat\partial_F f(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid \liminf_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\x\ne\bar x}}\frac{f(x)-f(\bar x)-\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle}{\|x-\bar x\|}\ge0\right\}.
\]
The quotient is interpreted in the extended-real sense. Equivalently, \(v\in\widehat\partial_F f(\bar x)\) if and only if \(f(x)\ge f(\bar x)+\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle+o(\|x-\bar x\|)\) as \(x\to\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Fréchet subgradient gives a first-order local lower approximation whose error is negligible relative to displacement.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) finite at \(\bar x\), the regular subdifferential is

\widehat\partial f(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid f(x)\ge f(\bar x)+\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle+o(\|x-\bar x\|)\ \text{as }x\to\bar x\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, membership means that for every \(\eta>0\), some \(\delta>0\) satisfies \(f(x)\ge f(\bar x)+\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle-\eta\|x-\bar x\|\) whenever \(\|x-\bar x\|<\delta\).

knowledge_statements.title: Fréchet–Regular Coincidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminological coincidence under the standard finite-dimensional lower-subdifferential convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be finite at \(\bar x\). When the Fréchet and regular lower subdifferentials are both defined by the first-order condition
\[
\liminf_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\x\ne\bar x}}\frac{f(x)-f(\bar x)-\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle}{\|x-\bar x\|}\ge 0,
\]
they coincide:
\[
\widehat\partial_F f(\bar x)=\widehat\partial f(\bar x).
\]
Thus “Fréchet” and “regular” name the same lower subdifferential under this convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite-dimensional variational analysis, the Fréchet and regular lower subdifferentials are the same object when both use the standard first-order lower-approximation convention.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb{R}\).
Both symbols use the lower first-order quotient convention in Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\partial_F f(\bar x)=\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\in\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\iff(v,-1)\in\widehat N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\).

notation.meaning: Fréchet regular normal cone to a set C at z.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph-normal representation of regular subgradients in Euclidean space.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.1 Basic Definitions and Representations p. 40

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\) with \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb{R}\), and let \(\widehat N\) denote the Fréchet regular normal cone. Then
\[
v\in\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (v,-1)\in\widehat N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x)).
\]
Consequently, regular subgradients are exactly the horizontal components of regular epigraph normals whose vertical component is normalized to \(-1\). This identifies first-order lower support of \(f\) with regular normal geometry of its epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is a regular subgradient exactly when adjoining vertical component minus one produces a regular normal to the epigraph.
knowledge_statements.title: Regular Subgradient Geometry

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.1 Basic Definitions and Representations p. 40

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional lower-Hadamard directional characterization and resulting convex geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be finite at \(\bar x\), and define
\[
df(\bar x)(w):=\liminf_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\w'\to w}}\frac{f(\bar x+t w')-f(\bar x)}{t}.
\]
Then
\[
\widehat\partial f(\bar x)=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle v,w\rangle\le df(\bar x)(w)\ \text{for every }w\in\mathbb{R}^n\right\}.
\]
Consequently, \(\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\) is closed and convex, possibly empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regular subgradients are exactly the linear functionals dominated in every direction by the lower Hadamard directional derivative; consequently the regular subdifferential is closed and convex, though it may be empty.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\)\) is finite at \(\bar x\).
\(df(\bar x)\) denotes the lower Hadamard directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\partial f(\bar x)=\{v:\langle v,w\rangle\le df(\bar x)(w)\ \forall w\}\), and this set is closed and convex.

notation.meaning: lower Hadamard directional derivative of f at the reference point in direction w

knowledge_statements.title: Directional Characterization of Regular Subgradients

children.title: Fréchet Epsilon-Subgradients
children.top_down_role: Approximate regular subgradients used in sequential representations.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\partial_\varepsilon f(\bar x)\) permits a first-order lower error of at most \(\varepsilon\|x-\bar x\|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional lower Fréchet epsilon-subdifferential with additive slope tolerance.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.2 Frechet-Like \( \varepsilon \)-Subgradients and Limiting Representations p. 87
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(\varepsilon\ge0\), define
\[
\widehat\partial_\varepsilon f(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid \liminf_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\x\ne\bar x}}\frac{f(x)-f(\bar x)-\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle}{\|x-\bar x\|}\ge-\varepsilon\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(v\in\widehat\partial_\varepsilon f(\bar x)\) when \(f(x)\ge f(\bar x)+\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle-(\varepsilon+o(1))\|x-\bar x\|\) as \(x\to\bar x\). For \(\varepsilon=0\), this reduces to the Fréchet subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epsilon-subgradient is a Fréchet subgradient whose local first-order support inequality may lose epsilon times the displacement.
knowledge_statements.title: Fréchet Epsilon-Subgradients

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3.2 Frechet-Like \( \varepsilon \)-Subgradients and Limiting Representations p. 87
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Tolerance Is Not a Minkowski Enlargement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Downward cusp showing that positive tolerance can create approximate regular subgradients even when the exact regular subdifferential is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=-|x|\) at \(0\),
\[
\widehat\partial_\varepsilon f(0)=
\begin{cases}
\varnothing,&0\le\varepsilon<1,\\
[1-\varepsilon,\,\varepsilon-1],&\varepsilon\ge1.
\end{cases}
\]
In particular, \(\widehat\partial f(0)=\varnothing\), whereas \(\widehat\partial_1f(0)=\{0\}\). Hence, in general,
\[
\widehat\partial_\varepsilon f(\bar x)\ne\widehat\partial f(\bar x)+\varepsilon\mathbb B.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the downward cusp the exact regular subdifferential is empty, but sufficiently large tolerance produces epsilon-subgradients. Thus the epsilon-subdifferential is not generally an epsilon-ball enlargement of the exact regular subdifferential.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) is given by \(f(x)=-|x|\).
\(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\partial_\varepsilon f(0)=\varnothing\) for \(\varepsilon<1\) and \([1-\varepsilon,\varepsilon-1]\) for \(\varepsilon\ge1\); hence the Minkowski-enlargement formula fails in general.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Tolerance Is Not a Minkowski Enlargement

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometry and Monotonicity of Fréchet Epsilon-Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional structural properties of the tolerance-indexed family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be finite at \(\bar x\). For every \(\varepsilon\ge0\),
\[
\widehat\partial_\varepsilon f(\bar x)=\left\{v:\langle v,w\rangle\le df(\bar x)(w)+\varepsilon\|w\|\ \text{for all }w\in\mathbb{R}^n\right\},
\]
where \(df\) is the lower Hadamard directional derivative. Thus every \(\widehat\partial_\varepsilon f(\bar x)\) is closed and convex, and
\[
0\le\varepsilon_1\le\varepsilon_2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\widehat\partial_{\varepsilon_1}f(\bar x)\subseteq\widehat\partial_{\varepsilon_2}f(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epsilon-subdifferential consists of linear functionals dominated by the lower directional derivative up to epsilon times direction length. Its values are closed, convex, and nested as epsilon increases.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\)\) is finite at \(\bar x\).
\(0\le\varepsilon_1\le\varepsilon_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each \(\widehat\partial_\varepsilon f(\bar x)\) is closed and convex, and \(\widehat\partial_{\varepsilon_1}f(\bar x)\subseteq\widehat\partial_{\varepsilon_2}f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Geometry and Monotonicity of Fréchet Epsilon-Subdifferentials

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) finite at \(\bar x\), define the limiting subdifferential by
\[
\partial_L f(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid \exists x_k\to\bar x,\ f(x_k)\to f(\bar x),\ \exists v_k\to v:\ v_k\in\widehat\partial f(x_k)\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, with \(x\to_f\bar x\) denoting simultaneous point and function-value convergence,
\[
\partial_L f(\bar x)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{x\to_f\bar x}\widehat\partial f(x).
\]
No convexification is performed in this outer limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting subdifferential consists of limits of regular subgradients at nearby points with convergent function values.

x_k\to\bar x,\quad f(x_k)\to f(\bar x),\quad v_k\to v,\quad v_k\in\partial_L f(x_k),
\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) finite at \(\bar x\), the Mordukhovich, or basic, subdifferential is
\[
\partial_M f(\bar x):=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\f(x)\to f(\bar x)}}\widehat\partial f(x).
\]
Thus \(v\in\partial_M f(\bar x)\) precisely when sequences \(x_k\to\bar x\) and \(v_k\to v\) exist such that \(f(x_k)\to f(\bar x)\) and \(v_k\in\widehat\partial f(x_k)\) for all \(k\). The construction retains nonconvex first-order information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Mordukhovich subdifferential is the unconvexified outer limit of nearby regular subdifferentials under function-value convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Mordukhovich Subdifferential

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be finite at \(\bar x\). Under the standard finite-dimensional definitions, the limiting subdifferential and the Mordukhovich basic subdifferential coincide:
\[
\partial_L f(\bar x)=\partial_M f(\bar x)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\f(x)\to f(\bar x)}}\widehat\partial f(x).
\]
Both sides therefore consist of exactly the strong limits \(v_k\to v\) of regular subgradients \(v_k\in\widehat\partial f(x_k)\) along sequences satisfying \(x_k\to\bar x\) and \(f(x_k)\to f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, “limiting” and “Mordukhovich basic” denote the same unconvexified sequential subdifferential.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Subgradient Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete one-dimensional illustration of unconvexified limiting structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) finite at \(\bar x\), the regular and Mordukhovich subdifferentials satisfy
\[
\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\subseteq\partial_M f(\bar x).
\]
The inclusion can be strict, and the Mordukhovich subdifferential need not be convex. For the locally Lipschitz function \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) defined by \(f(x)=-|x|\),
\[
\widehat\partial f(0)=\varnothing,\qquad \partial_M f(0)=\{-1,1\}.
\]
This example displays the unconvexified structure of the basic limiting construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regular subdifferential is contained in the limiting one, but the inclusion can be strict and the limiting set can be nonconvex; for minus absolute value at zero it is the two-point set consisting of minus one and one.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb{R}\) for the general inclusion.
For the example, \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) is defined by \(f(x)=-|x|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\subseteq\partial_M f(\bar x)\), and for \(f(x)=-|x|\), \(\widehat\partial f(0)=\varnothing\) while \(\partial_M f(0)=\{-1,1\}\).

children.title: Clarke Subdifferential
children.top_down_role: Convexified generalized gradients in locally Lipschitz regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Clarke Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional locally Lipschitz definition and limiting-subgradient representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Clarke subdifferential of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) is
\[
\partial^C f(\bar x):=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle v,d\rangle\leq f^\circ(\bar x;d)\ \text{for every }d\in\mathbb{R}^n\},
\]
where
\[
f^\circ(\bar x;d):=\limsup_{x\to\bar x,\,t\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t}.
\]
For locally Lipschitz \(f\), the set \(\partial^C f(\bar x)\) is nonempty, compact, and convex, and
\[
\partial^C f(\bar x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}\partial f(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke subdifferential consists of the vectors dominated by the Clarke generalized directional derivative. For a locally Lipschitz function, it is a nonempty compact convex set equal to the closed convex hull of the limiting subdifferential.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^C f(\bar x)\) is a nonempty compact convex set and equals \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}\partial f(\bar x)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual equivalence between the Clarke generalized directional derivative and Clarke subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(d\in\mathbb R^n\),
\[
f^\circ(\bar x;d)=\max_{v\in\partial^C f(\bar x)}\langle v,d\rangle
=\sigma_{\partial^C f(\bar x)}(d).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke generalized directional derivative is the support function of the Clarke subdifferential.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^\circ(\bar x;d)=\sigma_{\partial^C f(\bar x)}(d)\) for every \(d\).
knowledge_statements.title: Support-Function Characterization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stability of the finite-dimensional Clarke-subdifferential mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There are a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(L<\infty\) such that
\[
\partial^C f(x)\subseteq L\mathbb B\quad(x\in U).
\]
If \(x_k\to x\in U\), \(v_k\to v\), and \(v_k\in\partial^C f(x_k)\), then \(v\in\partial^C f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a locally Lipschitz point, Clarke subgradients are uniformly bounded and the Clarke-subdifferential mapping is upper semicontinuous.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mapping \(x\mapsto\partial^C f(x)\) is locally bounded and upper semicontinuous near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.title: Upper Semicontinuity and Local Boundedness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional representation through gradients at nearby differentiability points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D_f\) be the differentiability set of \(f\) and
\[
G_f(\bar x):=\left\{\lim_{k\to\infty}\nabla f(x_k):x_k\to\bar x,\ x_k\in D_f\right\}.
\]
Then
\[
\partial^C f(\bar x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}G_f(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke subdifferential is the closed convex hull of limits of gradients at nearby differentiability points.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^C f(\bar x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}G_f(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: set of differentiability points of f
reachable gradient limits at the reference point

children.title: Subdifferential Inclusions
children.top_down_role: Containment relations among regular, limiting, convex, and Clarke systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential Inclusions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional locally Lipschitz hierarchy at a finite-valued reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a proper lower-semicontinuous function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) that is finite at \(\bar x\),
\[
\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\subseteq\partial f(\bar x).
\]
If \(f\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\), then
\[
\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\subseteq\partial f(\bar x)\subseteq\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}\partial f(\bar x)=\partial^C f(\bar x).
\]
For nonregular nonconvex functions, either successive inclusion can be strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regular subgradients are limiting subgradients. If the function is locally Lipschitz near the reference point, limiting subgradients lie in the Clarke subdifferential; either successive inclusion can be strict for a nonregular nonconvex function.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper and lower semicontinuous with \(f(\bar x)<+\infty\).
For the inclusion involving \(\partial^C f(\bar x)\), \(f\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\subseteq\partial f(\bar x)\), and under local Lipschitz continuity, \(\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\subseteq\partial f(\bar x)\subseteq\partial^C f(\bar x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Subdifferential regularity of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) entails
\[
\widehat\partial f(\bar x)=\partial f(\bar x).
\]
If, additionally, \(f\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) and \(\partial f(\bar x)\) is closed and convex, then Clarke convexification introduces no enlargement and
\[
\widehat\partial f(\bar x)=\partial f(\bar x)=\partial^C f(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a subdifferentially regular point, regular and limiting subdifferentials coincide. Local Lipschitz continuity and convexity of that set also yield Clarke coincidence.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singleton coincidence under strict differentiability in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f\) is strictly differentiable at \(\bar x\), then
\[
\widehat\partial f(\bar x)=\partial f(\bar x)=\partial^C f(\bar x)=\{\nabla f(\bar x)\}.
\]
In particular, the conclusion holds when \(f\) is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict differentiability collapses the regular, limiting, and Clarke subdifferentials to the classical gradient singleton; local continuous differentiability is a standard sufficient condition.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is strictly differentiable at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\partial f(\bar x)=\partial f(\bar x)=\partial^C f(\bar x)=\{\nabla f(\bar x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Differentiability Coincidence Regime

children.top_down_role: Specialization of generalized subgradients under convexity.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex with \(f(\bar x)<+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All standard regular, limiting, and convex subdifferentials coincide at \(\bar x\); when \(f\) is locally Lipschitz there, the Clarke subdifferential also coincides.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions in finite dimensions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function,
\[
\widehat\partial f(\bar x)=\partial f(\bar x)=\partial_{\mathrm{cvx}}f(\bar x)
=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(x)\geq f(\bar x)+\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle\ \text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^n\}.
\]
If \(f\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\), then this common closed convex set also equals \(\partial^C f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper closed convex function, regular, limiting, and convex subdifferentials agree; local Lipschitz continuity adds the Clarke subdifferential to the coincidence.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Coincidence Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential Separation Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical one-dimensional strict-separation example.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) defined by \(f(x)=-|x|\),
\[
\widehat\partial f(0)=\varnothing\subsetneq\partial f(0)=\{-1,1\}\subsetneq\partial^C f(0)=[-1,1].
\]
Thus both successive inclusions in the regular–limiting–Clarke hierarchy are strict at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the downward cusp given by minus the absolute value, the regular subdifferential at zero is empty, the limiting subdifferential consists of minus one and one, and the Clarke subdifferential is the interval between them. Both successive inclusions are strict.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) is given by \(f(x)=-|x|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \(0\), \(\widehat\partial f(0)=\varnothing\), \(\partial f(0)=\{-1,1\}\), and \(\partial^C f(0)=[-1,1]\).

children.top_down_role: Horizontal-normal representations of singular or horizon subgradients.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper and lower semicontinuous with \(f(\bar x)<+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)=\{v:(v,0)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The horizon subdifferential of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) is represented by horizontal limiting normals to its epigraph:
\[
\partial^\infty f(\bar x):=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:(v,0)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\},
\]
where \(\operatorname{epi}f:=\{(x,r)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}:r\geq f(x)\}\). The zero last coordinate distinguishes horizon subgradients from ordinary subgradients, which correspond to normals of the form \((v,-1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Horizon subgradients are exactly the horizontal limiting normals to the function's epigraph at the point on its graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Horizontal Epigraph Representations

children.title: Local Lipschitz Regularity
children.top_down_role: Local finite-slope behavior relevant to horizontal subgradients.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(\bar x\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local Lipschitz regularity means that \(|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L\|x-y\|\) holds for all \(x,y\) in some neighborhood of \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: a neighborhood of the reference point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard finite-dimensional local Lipschitz condition.

source_refs.locator: 4.3 Subdifferentials and Regularity p. 170
source_refs.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is locally Lipschitz around \(\bar x\) if there exist an open neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and a constant \(L\geq0\) such that
\[
|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L\|x-y\|\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in U.
\]
In particular, \(f\) is finite and continuous throughout a possibly smaller neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is locally Lipschitz around a point when one uniform Lipschitz bound holds for every pair of points in a neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Lipschitz Regularity

children.title: Horizontal Subdifferential Vanishing
children.top_down_role: Triviality of the horizontal subgradient component.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vanishing of finite-dimensional horizon subgradients under local Lipschitz regularity.

source_refs.locator: 2.4.2 Representations of Singular Subgradients and Horizontal Normals to Graphs and Epigraphs p. 223

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f\) is locally Lipschitz on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\), then its epigraph has no nonzero horizontal limiting normal at \((\bar x,f(\bar x))\). Equivalently,
\[
\partial^\infty f(\bar x)=\{0\}.
\]
Thus every horizon subgradient at \(\bar x\) vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local Lipschitz continuity eliminates nonzero horizontal epigraph normals, so the horizon subdifferential contains only zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Horizontal Subdifferential Vanishing

children.title: Lipschitz-to-Vanishing Passage
children.top_down_role: Connection from local Lipschitz behavior to horizontal triviality.

knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz-to-Vanishing Passage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential mechanism behind Lipschitz-to-horizon vanishing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\), then every regular subgradient \(v\in\widehat\partial f(x)\) at a sufficiently nearby point \(x\) satisfies \(\|v\|\leq L\). Consequently, whenever \(x_k\to\bar x\), \(f(x_k)\to f(\bar x)\), \(v_k\in\widehat\partial f(x_k)\), and \(\lambda_k\downarrow0\),
\[
\lambda_kv_k\longrightarrow0.
\]
Thus every limit admitted by the sequential horizon construction is zero, and
\[
\partial^\infty f(\bar x)=\{0\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a locally Lipschitz function, nearby regular subgradients are uniformly bounded by the Lipschitz modulus. Scaling any such sequence by positive scalars tending to zero gives only the zero horizon limit.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
\(x_k\to\bar x\), \(f(x_k)\to f(\bar x)\), \(v_k\in\widehat\partial f(x_k)\), and \(\lambda_k\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_kv_k\to0\) for every such sequence, and hence \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)=\{0\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For proper lower-semicontinuous functions on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), the standard finite-dimensional criterion identifies local Lipschitz regularity around \(\bar x\) with
\[
\partial^\infty f(\bar x)=\{0\},
\]
subject to the usual local epigraphical hypotheses. This converse must not be transferred unchanged to general infinite-dimensional Banach spaces: compactness or sequential normal-compactness assumptions are needed to convert absence of nonzero horizon limits into a uniform local Lipschitz bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Horizon vanishing supports a converse Lipschitz criterion in finite dimensions, but a general Banach-space converse needs additional compactness or normal-compactness hypotheses.

children.title: Singular Qualification Role
children.top_down_role: Use of horizontal subgradients in calculus qualifications and abnormality tests.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional no-abnormal-cancellation condition and its role in limiting-subdifferential sum calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\). The singular qualification at \(\bar x\) is
\[
\left[v_i\in\partial^\infty f_i(\bar x),\ \sum_{i=1}^m v_i=0\right]\Longrightarrow v_1=\cdots=v_m=0.
\]
If each \(f_i\) is lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\) and finite there, this qualification yields the finite-dimensional limiting sum-rule inclusion
\[
\partial F(\bar x)\subseteq\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The qualification excludes cancellation among nonzero horizon subgradients. For finitely many lower-semicontinuous summands in finite dimensions, it validates the limiting-subdifferential sum inclusion.
assumptions_latex: \(f_i:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), are lower semicontinuous on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\) and finite at \(\bar x\).
Whenever \(v_i\in\partial^\infty f_i(\bar x)\) and \(\sum_i v_i=0\), every \(v_i\) is zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(\sum_{i=1}^m f_i)(\bar x)\subseteq\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: horizon subdifferential of the ith summand
limiting subdifferential of the ith summand

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sum Singular Qualification

assumptions_latex: \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), are proper lower-semicontinuous functions finite at \(\bar x\).
Whenever \(v_i\in\partial^\infty f_i(\bar x)\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^m v_i=0\), one has \(v_i=0\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The horizon qualification excludes abnormal cancellation and supports the limiting sum-rule inclusion \(\partial(\sum_i f_i)(\bar x)\subseteq\sum_i\partial f_i(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: horizon subdifferential of the ith summand

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sum horizon qualification for limiting-subdifferential calculus.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Generalized Differentiation in Banach Spaces p. 3
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A standard singular qualification for the finite sum \(F:=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\) is
\[
\left[v_i\in\partial^\infty f_i(\bar x),\ \sum_{i=1}^m v_i=0\right]\Longrightarrow\left[v_1=\cdots=v_m=0\right].
\]
It rules out cancellation among nonzero abnormal multipliers. Under the accompanying hypotheses of the limiting sum rule, this condition yields
\[
\partial F(\bar x)\subseteq\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular qualification forbids nonzero horizon subgradients from canceling. Under the sum-rule hypotheses, this validates decomposition of each limiting subgradient into summand subgradients.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular Qualification Role

children.title: Piecewise Linear–Quadratic Subdifferentials
children.top_down_role: Finite-piece polyhedral and quadratic subgradient geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise Linear–Quadratic Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex finite-maximum piecewise linear–quadratic functions with a common quadratic term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be symmetric positive semidefinite, define
\[
q_i(x):=\tfrac12\langle x,Qx\rangle+\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\quad (i=1,\ldots,m),
\]
and set
\[
f(x):=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}q_i(x),\qquad I(x):=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:q_i(x)=f(x)\}.
\]
Then \(f\) is a convex piecewise linear–quadratic function and
\[
\partial f(x)=\operatorname{co}\{Qx+a_i:i\in I(x)\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a maximum of finitely many convex quadratics sharing the same quadratic term, the function is convex piecewise linear–quadratic, and its subdifferential is the convex hull of the gradients of its active pieces.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
For some \(\rho\ge 0\), the function \(x\mapsto f(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\|x\|^2\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)=\partial\!\left(f+\frac{\rho}{2}\|\cdot\|^2\right)(x)-\rho x\), with the displayed global quadratic support inequality.

notation.meaning: Limiting subdifferential of f at x; it agrees here with the shifted convex subdifferential.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), set \(g=f+\frac{\rho}{2}\|\cdot\|^2\). Then \[\partial f(x)=\partial g(x)-\rho x.\] Equivalently, \(v\in\partial f(x)\) if and only if \[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle v,y-x\rangle-\frac{\rho}{2}\|y-x\|^2\qquad\text{for every }y\in\mathbb{R}^n.\] Thus the subdifferential of a weakly convex function consists exactly of its global quadratic-support slopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weakly convex function has subgradients exactly when it admits global affine supports with a quadratic downward correction.

assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=\cos x\) on \(\mathbb R\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of convex-style optimality for a positive weak-convexity modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\cos x\), the function \(f+\frac12|\cdot|^2\) is convex, so \(f\) is \(1\)-weakly convex. Moreover, \(0\in\partial f(0)=\{0\}\), although \(0\) is a strict local maximum and is not a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero subgradient of a weakly convex function certifies stationarity, not minimality.

knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Convex Stationarity Need Not Certify a Minimum

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(f+\frac\rho2\|\cdot\|^2\) is convex for some \(\rho\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f+\rho I\) is maximally monotone and \(\langle v-w,x-y\rangle\ge-\rho\|x-y\|^2\) for all graph pairs.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional operator structure inherited from the convex quadratic shift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is \(\rho\)-weakly convex, then \(\partial f+\rho I=\partial(f+\frac\rho2\|\cdot\|^2)\) is maximally monotone. Consequently, for every \((x,v),(y,w)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\), \[\langle v-w,x-y\rangle\ge-\rho\|x-y\|^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting subdifferential of a rho-weakly convex function is rho-hypomonotone, and its rho-shift is maximally monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hypomonotonicity of the Weakly Convex Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.title: Hypomonotonicity of the Weakly Convex Subdifferential

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise subdifferential structure inherited from the convex quadratic shift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \[\partial_Pf(x)=\widehat\partial f(x)=\partial f(x)=\partial_c\!\left(f+\tfrac\rho2\|\cdot\|^2\right)(x)-\rho x.\] This set is closed and convex, although it can be empty at boundary points of \(\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a weakly convex function, proximal, regular, and limiting subdifferentials coincide with a translated convex subdifferential.

children.title: Prox-Regular Subdifferentials
children.top_down_role: Subgradient geometry under prox-regularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Regular Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subgradient-attentive finite-dimensional prox-regularity at a specified graph pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is prox-regular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) if there exist \(r\ge 0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \[f(x')\ge f(x)+\langle v,x'-x\rangle-\frac r2\|x'-x\|^2\] whenever \(\|x-\bar x\|<\varepsilon\), \(\|x'-\bar x\|<\varepsilon\), \(|f(x)-f(\bar x)|<\varepsilon\), and \(v\in\partial f(x)\) satisfies \(\|v-\bar v\|<\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prox-regularity requires a uniform local quadratic lower support for nearby subgradients whose base points, function values, and slopes approach the reference graph pair.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\((\bar x,\bar v)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated localized quadratic-support inequality defines prox-regularity of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hypomonotonicity on the subgradient-attentive localization used in prox-regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For graph pairs \((x_i,v_i)\), \(i=1,2\), in a sufficiently small subgradient-attentive localization of \((\bar x,\bar v)\), prox-regularity with parameter \(r\) implies \(\langle v_1-v_2,x_1-x_2\rangle\ge-r\|x_1-x_2\|^2\). Equivalently, the localized mapping \(x\mapsto\partial f(x)+rx\) is monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A prox-regular subdifferential is locally hypomonotone around the designated graph pair.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is prox-regular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) with parameter \(r\).
Both graph pairs lie in the defining attentive localization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \langle v_1-v_2,x_1-x_2\rangle\ge-r\|x_1-x_2\|^2.
knowledge_statements.title: Localized Hypomonotonicity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local, not global, proximal stability around a prox-regular graph pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is additionally prox-bounded and subdifferentially continuous at \((\bar x,\bar v)\), then for sufficiently small \(\lambda>0\) with \(\lambda r<1\), an attentive localization of \((I+\lambda\partial f)^{-1}\) around \((\bar x+\lambda\bar v,\bar x)\) is single-valued and Lipschitz. The associated localized Moreau envelope is \(C^1\) and satisfies \(\nabla e_\lambda f(z)=\lambda^{-1}(z-P_\lambda f(z))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With prox-boundedness and subdifferential continuity, prox-regularity yields a locally single-valued proximal map and smooth local Moreau envelope.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, prox-bounded, prox-regular, and subdifferentially continuous at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\).
\(0<\lambda<1/r\), with \(1/0=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_\lambda f=(I+\lambda\partial f)^{-1}\text{ has a single-valued Lipschitz localization, and }\nabla e_\lambda f=\lambda^{-1}(I-P_\lambda f).
knowledge_statements.title: Localized Proximal Stability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the converse from prox-regularity to global weak convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The \(C^2\) function \(f(x)=-x^4\) is prox-regular at every graph pair \((\bar x,f'(\bar x))\), because its curvature is bounded below locally. However, \(f''(x)=-12x^2\) is unbounded below, so \(f+(\rho/2)|\cdot|^2\) is nonconvex for every finite \(\rho\). Hence prox-regularity does not imply global weak convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prox-regularity is local and does not imply global weak convexity; minus x to the fourth separates the classes.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=-x^4\) on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is prox-regular at every }(\bar x,f'(\bar x))\text{ but is not globally weakly convex}.

knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Regularity Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A downward cusp violates every finite local quadratic-support modulus at either limiting subgradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=-|x|\), the limiting subdifferential at the origin is \(\partial f(0)=\{-1,1\}\). The function \(f\) is not prox-regular at \(0\) for either \(v=1\) or \(v=-1\): no finite quadratic parameter gives the required local lower-support inequality at either graph pair \((0,1)\) or \((0,-1)\). Thus local Lipschitz continuity and lower semicontinuity do not by themselves imply prox-regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The downward cusp minus absolute value is locally Lipschitz and lower semicontinuous but fails prox-regularity at the origin for either limiting slope.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) is given by \(f(x)=-|x|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(\partial f(0)=\{-1,1\}\), the function is not prox-regular at \(0\) for either limiting subgradient.

children.title: Difference-of-Convex Subdifferentials
children.top_down_role: Subgradient structures associated with convex differences.

assumptions_latex: \(g,h:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper convex functions and are finite near \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The decomposition generates \(\partial g(x)-\partial h(x)\); if \(h\) is differentiable at \(x\), then \(\partial f(x)=\partial g(x)-\nabla h(x)\).

notation.meaning: Minkowski difference of the two convex subdifferential sets.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decomposition-dependent DC subgradient structure and its exact smooth-concave-part specialization.

source_refs.locator: 4.4.4 Difference-of-convex functions p. 224
source_refs.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The chosen DC decomposition associates with \(f\) the set \[\partial g(x)-\partial h(x)=\{u-w:u\in\partial g(x),\ w\in\partial h(x)\}.\] This set depends on the decomposition and is used in the DC criticality condition \(0\in\partial g(x)-\partial h(x)\). If \(h\) is differentiable at \(x\), the limiting-subdifferential smooth-perturbation rule gives the intrinsic identity \[\partial f(x)=\partial g(x)-\nabla h(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A DC decomposition yields differences of convex subgradients; this equals the intrinsic limiting subdifferential when the subtracted convex term is differentiable.
knowledge_statements.title: Difference-of-Convex Subdifferentials

source_witnesses.locator: 4.4.4 Difference-of-convex functions p. 224
source_witnesses.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary directional stationarity for a finite-valued DC decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\bar x\) locally minimizes \(g-h\), then \(g'(\bar x;d)\ge h'(\bar x;d)\) for every \(d\). For finite convex components this is equivalent to \(\partial h(\bar x)\subseteq\partial g(\bar x)\), which is generally stronger than DC criticality \(\partial g(\bar x)\cap\partial h(\bar x)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local minimizer of a finite DC function must contain the subtracted component's subdifferential in that of the first component.
assumptions_latex: The functions \(g,h\) are convex and finite near \(\bar x\).
\(f=g-h\), and \(\bar x\) is a local minimizer of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g'(\bar x;d)\ge h'(\bar x;d)\ \forall d\iff\partial h(\bar x)\subseteq\partial g(\bar x).
knowledge_statements.title: DC Directional Stationarity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of decomposition-dependent DC criticality as an optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(g(x)=0\), \(h(x)=|x|\), and \(f=g-h=-|x|\), one has \(0\in\partial g(0)-\partial h(0)\). Thus \(0\) is DC-critical, although it is a strict local maximum of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DC criticality can hold at a strict local maximum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in\partial g(0)-\partial h(0),\quad 0\text{ is not a local minimizer of }f.
knowledge_statements.title: DC Criticality Is Not Sufficient

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I(x)=\{i:f_i(x)=f(x)\}\). The finite maximum is subdifferentially regular at \(x\), and its limiting and Clarke subdifferentials coincide: \[\partial f(x)=\partial_C f(x)=\operatorname{co}\{\nabla f_i(x):i\in I(x)\}.\] Only gradients of active pieces enter the convex-hull representation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order stationarity for a finite smooth maximum and its convex sufficiency boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The condition \(0\in\partial f(\bar x)\) is equivalent to the existence of \(\lambda_i\ge0\), \(i\in I(\bar x)\), with \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\) and \(\sum_i\lambda_i\nabla f_i(\bar x)=0\). It is necessary at a local minimizer and sufficient for global minimality when all pieces are convex. Without convexity it is not sufficient; for example, \(\max\{-x^2,-2x^2\}=-x^2\) is stationary at its strict local maximum \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stationarity of a smooth finite maximum is a convex balance of active gradients; it is sufficient under convexity but not generally.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
\(f=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in\partial f(\bar x)\iff\exists\lambda\in\Delta_{I(\bar x)}:\sum_{i\in I(\bar x)}\lambda_i\nabla f_i(\bar x)=0.

notation.meaning: Simplex of weights supported on the active indices.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I(x)=\{i:f_i(x)=f(x)\}\). Then every limiting subgradient is an active gradient: \[\partial f(x)\subseteq\{\nabla f_i(x):i\in I(x)\}.\] If, for every \(i\in I(x)\), there are points \(x_k\to x\) at which \(i\) is the unique minimizing index, then \[\partial f(x)=\{\nabla f_i(x):i\in I(x)\}.\] Unlike the maximum rule, no convex hull is generally valid for the limiting subdifferential.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite smooth minimum; reachable gradients are limits at nearby differentiability points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G(\bar x)\) be the set of limits of classical gradients \(\nabla f(x_k)\) at differentiability points \(x_k\to\bar x\). Then \(G(\bar x)\subseteq\{\nabla f_i(\bar x):i\in I(\bar x)\}\), \(\partial f(\bar x)=G(\bar x)\), and \(\partial_Cf(\bar x)=\operatorname{co}G(\bar x)\). \(f=\min_i f_i\).

children.top_down_role: Subgradient behavior for functions assembled through local selections.

assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), is continuously differentiable near \(x\).
The locally Lipschitz function \(f\) is a continuous selection: \(f(z)\in\{f_1(z),\ldots,f_m(z)\}\) near \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial_C f(x)\subseteq\operatorname{co}\{\nabla f_i(x):i\in I(x)\}\).

notation.meaning: Pieces whose value agrees with the selection at x.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarke subdifferential containment for a locally Lipschitz continuous finite selection.

source_refs.locator: 4.3 Subdifferentials and Regularity p. 170

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(I(x)=\{i:f_i(x)=f(x)\}\). At every differentiability point \(z\) of \(f\) sufficiently near \(x\), its gradient equals the gradient of a locally selected active piece. Consequently, \[\partial_C f(x)\subseteq\operatorname{co}\{\nabla f_i(x):i\in I(x)\}.\] Equality need not hold because some value-matching pieces may never be selected on a nearby region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke subdifferential of a smooth-piece selection lies in the convex hull of gradients of value-matching pieces, possibly strictly.

source_witnesses.locator: 4.3 Subdifferentials and Regularity p. 170

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Locally Lipschitz continuous finite selection of smooth pieces.

knowledge_statements.title: Paratingent Graphical Derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional paratingent derivative defined through moving graph base points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Z\) be a finite-dimensional normed space, let \(C\subseteq Z\), and let \(z\in C\). Define
\[
T_C^P(z):=\left\{w\in Z:\exists z_k\to z,\ z_k\in C,\ t_k\downarrow0,\ w_k\to w,\ z_k+t_kw_k\in C\right\}.
\]
For \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\), the paratingent graphical derivative is
\[
D^PF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(h):=\left\{k\in Y:(h,k)\in T^P_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\right\},\qquad h\in X.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{gph}D^{P}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=T^{P}_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The paratingent graphical derivative consists of graph velocities obtained while the scale tends to zero and the graph base point approaches the reference graph point.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has locally closed graph near \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
\(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional normed spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}D^{P}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=T^{P}_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Tangential-Limit Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison under the standard inner, contingent, and paratingent tangent-cone conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=\operatorname{gph}F\) and \(z=(\bar x,\bar y)\). With
\[
T_C^i(z):=\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\frac{C-z}{t},\qquad T_C(z):=\limsup_{t\downarrow0}\frac{C-z}{t},
\]
and with \(T_C^P(z)\) formed by additionally allowing the base point in \(C\) to approach \(z\), one has
\[
T_C^i(z)\subseteq T_C(z)\subseteq T_C^P(z).
\]
Consequently,
\[
D^iF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(h)\subseteq DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(h)\subseteq D^PF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(h)
\]
for every \(h\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every inner graph velocity is a contingent graph velocity, and every contingent graph velocity is a paratingent graph velocity.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional graphical-convergence definition for a set-valued mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(t>0\), define the difference-quotient mapping by
\[
\Delta_tF(h):=\frac{F(\bar x+th)-\bar y}{t}.
\]
The mapping \(F\) is proto-differentiable at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar y\) when the graphs \(\operatorname{gph}\Delta_tF\) have a Painleve-Kuratowski limit as \(t\downarrow0\), equivalently when their inner and outer graphical limits coincide. The mapping whose graph is this common limit is the proto-derivative:
\[
\operatorname{gph}F'_{\bar x,\bar y}:=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\operatorname{gph}\Delta_tF.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proto-differentiability means that the graphs of first-order difference-quotient mappings converge to one well-defined limiting graph.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is semidifferentiable at \(\bar x\), then \(h\mapsto f'(\bar x;h)\) is continuous and positively homogeneous, and \[T_{\operatorname{gph}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))=\{(h,f'(\bar x;h)):h\in\mathbb R^n\}.\] Thus \(Df(\bar x)(h)=\{f'(\bar x;h)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The semiderivative is a continuous positively homogeneous model whose graph is the graph tangent cone.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is Hadamard semidifferentiable at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Df(\bar x)(h)=\{f'(\bar x;h)\}\) for every \(h\).
knowledge_statements.title: Graphical Representation of the Semiderivative

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional chain rule for Hadamard semidifferentiable mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is semidifferentiable at \(\bar x\) and \(g\) is semidifferentiable at \(f(\bar x)\), then \(g\circ f\) is semidifferentiable at \(\bar x\) and \[(g\circ f)'(\bar x;h)=g'(f(\bar x);f'(\bar x;h)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compositions of semidifferentiable mappings are semidifferentiable, with composed directional models.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is semidifferentiable at \(\bar x\).
\(g:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^p\) is semidifferentiable at \(f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((g\circ f)'(\bar x;h)=g'(f(\bar x);f'(\bar x;h))\).
knowledge_statements.title: Semidifferentiable Chain Rule

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to Y\) is single-valued between finite-dimensional normed spaces.
\(\bar x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is semidifferentiable at \(\bar x\) when the stable directional limit \(f'(\bar x;h)\) exists for every \(h\in X\).

notation.meaning: Semiderivative of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) in direction \(h\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hadamard-stable directional definition for finite-dimensional single-valued mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(f\) is semidifferentiable at \(\bar x\) if, for every \(h\in X\), there exists \(f'(\bar x;h)\in Y\) such that
\[
\lim_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\h'\to h}}\frac{f(\bar x+th')-f(\bar x)}{t}=f'(\bar x;h).
\]
The perturbation \(h'\to h\) is part of the requirement. The resulting mapping \(h\mapsto f'(\bar x;h)\) is positively homogeneous, although it need not be additive or linear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mapping is semidifferentiable when every directional quotient has a limit stable under simultaneous small perturbations of the direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Semidifferentiability of Mappings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Hadamard-stable directional-limit definition is standard under some terminology conventions, but a dedicated source is required to confirm that this is the intended meaning of semidifferentiability here.

children.title: Graphical Regularity
children.top_down_role: Stable local behavior of graph-based derivative models.

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\to Y\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\), with finite-dimensional \(X,Y\).
The regular and limiting normals are taken at \((\bar x,F(\bar x))\) to the locally closed graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is graphically regular at \(\bar x\) exactly when \(\widehat N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,F(\bar x))=N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,F(\bar x))\).

notation.meaning: Regular and limiting normal cones, respectively.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-cone regularity of a locally Lipschitz mapping's graph.

source_refs.locator: 3.2.4 Graphical Regularity of Lipschitzian Mappings p. 327
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is graphically regular at \(\bar x\) when its graph is normally regular at \((\bar x,F(\bar x))\), namely when
\[
\widehat N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,F(\bar x))=N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,F(\bar x)).
\]
Here the left side is the regular normal cone and the right side is the limiting normal cone. Graphical regularity therefore excludes additional normals obtainable only as limits of regular normals at nearby graph points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz mapping is graphically regular when the regular and limiting normal cones to its graph coincide at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.title: Graphical Regularity

children.title: Strict Differentiability
children.top_down_role: Uniform first-order approximation under paired nearby-point perturbations.

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to Y\) is a mapping between finite-dimensional normed spaces.
\(\bar x\in X\) and \(A:X\to Y\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is strictly differentiable at \(\bar x\) with derivative \(A\) exactly when the two-point first-order remainder is \(o(\|x-u\|)\).

notation.meaning: Operator norm induced by the norms on \(X\) and \(Y\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional two-point, or strong, differentiability.

source_refs.locator: 3.2.4 Graphical Regularity of Lipschitzian Mappings p. 327
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(f\) is strictly differentiable at \(\bar x\) with strict derivative \(A\) if
\[
\lim_{\substack{x,u\to\bar x\\x\ne u}}\frac{\|f(x)-f(u)-A(x-u)\|}{\|x-u\|}=0.
\]
Equivalently, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that
\[
\|f(x)-f(u)-A(x-u)\|\leq\varepsilon\|x-u\|
\]
for all distinct \(x,u\in U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict differentiability uniformly approximates every nearby two-point increment by the same linear map, not merely increments based at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Differentiability

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2.4 Graphical Regularity of Lipschitzian Mappings p. 327
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Immediate finite-dimensional consequences of the two-point approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is strictly differentiable at \(\bar x\) with strict derivative \(A\), then \(A\) is unique, \(f\) is Fréchet differentiable at \(\bar x\) with \(f'(\bar x)=A\), and \(f\) is Lipschitz on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict differentiability gives a unique ordinary derivative and local Lipschitz continuity.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to Y\) is strictly differentiable at \(\bar x\) between finite-dimensional normed spaces with strict derivative \(A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A=f'(\bar x)\) uniquely, and \(f\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.title: Basic Consequences of Strict Differentiability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional locally Lipschitz characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a locally Lipschitz mapping \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), \[f\text{ is strictly differentiable at }\bar x\text{ with derivative }A\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\partial_Cf(\bar x)=\{A\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz mapping is strictly differentiable exactly when its Clarke generalized Jacobian is a singleton.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is strictly differentiable at \(\bar x\) with derivative \(A\iff\partial_Cf(\bar x)=\{A\}\).

notation.meaning: Unique generalized Jacobian matrix and strict derivative.

knowledge_statements.title: Clarke Singleton Characterization

children.title: Graphical-to-Strict Passage
children.top_down_role: Conditions linking stable graphical models to strict differentiability.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
Graphical regularity means equality of regular and limiting normals to \(\operatorname{gph}f\) at \((\bar x,f(\bar x))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Graphical regularity at \(\bar x\) implies strict differentiability of \(f\) at \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: Strict derivative supplied by the graphical-regularity conclusion.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional locally Lipschitz single-valued passage; exact source hypotheses require confirmation.

source_refs.locator: 3.2.4 Graphical Regularity of Lipschitzian Mappings p. 327
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) and
\[
\widehat N_{\operatorname{gph}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))=N_{\operatorname{gph}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x)).
\]
Then there exists a linear mapping \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) such that
\[
\lim_{\substack{x,u\to\bar x\\x\ne u}}\frac{\|f(x)-f(u)-A(x-u)\|}{\|x-u\|}=0.
\]
Thus, under local Lipschitz continuity, graphical regularity forces strict differentiability at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite-dimensional locally Lipschitz single-valued mapping, normal regularity of the graph forces a uniform two-point linear approximation.
knowledge_statements.title: Graphical-to-Strict Passage

children.title: Strictness Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Graphically regular regimes that do not yield strict differentiability.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(x)=x^2\sin(1/x)\) for \(x\ne0\).
Differentiability and strict differentiability are considered at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(0)=0\), but \(f\) is not strictly differentiable at \(0\).

notation.meaning: Ordinary derivative of \(f\) at the origin.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordinary differentiability does not imply strict differentiability, even under local Lipschitz continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
f(x):=\begin{cases}x^2\sin(1/x),&x\ne0,\\0,&x=0.\end{cases}
\]
Then \(f\) is locally Lipschitz and differentiable at \(0\), with \(f'(0)=0\), because \(f(x)/x\to0\). For \(x\ne0\),
\[
f'(x)=2x\sin(1/x)-\cos(1/x),
\]
which does not converge to \(0\) as \(x\to0\). Suitable nearby pairs therefore have difference quotients bounded away from \(0\), so
\[
\lim_{\substack{x,u\to0\\x\ne u}}\frac{|f(x)-f(u)|}{|x-u|}\ne0.
\]
Hence differentiability at the point does not ensure strict differentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz function may have a derivative at the reference point while nearby secant slopes continue to oscillate, preventing strict differentiability.
knowledge_statements.title: Strictness Failure Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example correctly targets the failure of strict differentiability and the failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but it has no citation and includes proof text. A sourced, proof-free candidate is required.
