children.title: Marginal Qualification Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Compactness, regularity, and attainment regimes controlling marginal calculus.

assumptions_latex: \(p(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}}\Phi(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[p(0)=1,\qquad p(x)=0\text{ for }x\ne0,\qquad S(x)=\{1/x\}\text{ for }x\ne0.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by escaping minimizers and loss of local level boundedness.

source_refs.locator: 5.1 Nonlinear Programming-Based Value Functions p. 254
source_refs.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\Phi(x,y)=(xy-1)^2\), direct minimization gives \[p(0)=1,\qquad p(x)=0\text{ for }x\ne0.\] Moreover, \(S(x)=\{1/x\}\) for \(x\ne0\), so minimizers escape to infinity as \(x\to0\). The value function is discontinuous at \(0\). Therefore smoothness of the integrand alone does not ensure marginal continuity or subdifferential sensitivity; local level boundedness, compactness, or an equivalent inner semicompactness condition is essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without local level boundedness, optimizers can escape to infinity and a smooth objective can produce a discontinuous marginal value.
knowledge_statements.title: Marginal Qualification Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: 5.1 Nonlinear Programming-Based Value Functions p. 254
source_witnesses.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal sequential compactness condition used to pass marginal subgradients through convergent active minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The argmin mapping \(S\) is value-attentively inner semicompact at \(\bar x\) if, whenever
\[x_k\to\bar x,\qquad p(x_k)\to p(\bar x),\qquad y_k\in S(x_k),\]
one can choose such minimizers so that a subsequence converges to some \(\bar y\in S(\bar x)\). Local uniform level-boundedness together with lower semicontinuity is a standard sufficient condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Marginal calculus needs convergent minimizing selections along value-attentive parameter sequences; local uniform level-boundedness is a convenient sufficient condition.
assumptions_latex: \(p(x)=\inf_y\Phi(x,y)\) and \(S(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_y\Phi(x,y)\).
The sequences considered satisfy \(x_k\to\bar x\) and \(p(x_k)\to p(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\exists\,y_k\in S(x_k),\ k_j\uparrow\infty,\ \bar y\in S(\bar x):\quad y_{k_j}\to\bar y.\]
knowledge_statements.title: Attentive Inner Semicompactness of Minimizers

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compactness condition preventing bounded-value decisions from escaping near the reference parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The integrand is level-bounded in \(y\) locally uniformly in \(x\) at \(\bar x\) if, for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), there are a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and a bounded set \(B\subset\mathbb R^m\) such that
\[\{y:\Phi(x,y)\le\alpha\}\subset B\qquad(x\in U).\]
For proper lower-semicontinuous \(\Phi\) with finite \(p(\bar x)\), this yields nonempty compact \(S(\bar x)\) and bounds every sequence \(y_k\) for which \(x_k\to\bar x\) and \(\sup_k\Phi(x_k,y_k)<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local uniform level-boundedness confines bounded-value decisions and yields compact attainment at the reference parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(p(x)=\inf_y\Phi(x,y)\), with \(p(\bar x)<\infty\).
\(\Phi\) is level-bounded in \(y\) locally uniformly in \(x\) at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[S(\bar x)\ne\varnothing\text{ is compact},\qquad x_k\to\bar x,\ \sup_k\Phi(x_k,y_k)<\infty\Rightarrow (y_k)\text{ is bounded}.\]
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Local Level-Boundedness

children.title: Integral-Functional Subdifferentiation
children.top_down_role: Subgradient interchange and aggregation for integral functionals.

assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)\) is a finite measure space, \(1\le p<\infty\), and \(q\) is conjugate to \(p\).
\(f:\Omega\times\mathbb{R}^d\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is a convex normal integrand, and \(I(x)=\int_\Omega f(\omega,x(\omega))\,d\mu\).
\(I\) is finite and continuous at some point of \(L^p(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^d)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\partial I(x)=\{\xi\in L^q:\xi(\omega)\in\partial f(\omega,x(\omega))\text{ for almost every }\omega\}.\]

notation.meaning: Integral functional on the Bochner space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex pointwise subgradient interchange on finite-measure Bochner spaces.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Generalized Differentiation in Banach Spaces p. 3
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^d)\) with \(I(x)<\infty\), a function \(\xi\in L^q(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^d)\) is a convex subgradient of \(I\) exactly when it is a measurable, integrable pointwise subgradient selection: \[\partial I(x)=\{\xi\in L^q(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^d):\xi(\omega)\in\partial f(\omega,x(\omega))\text{ for almost every }\omega\}.\] Thus subdifferentiation and integration interchange under the stated qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of a qualified convex integral functional consists exactly of integrable selections from the pointwise subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.title: Integral-Functional Subdifferentiation

knowledge_statements.title: Fuzzy Sum Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite fuzzy Fréchet-subdifferential sum rule in an Asplund space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\). For every \(x^*\in\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist \(x_i\in B_\varepsilon(\bar x)\) and \(x_i^*\in\widehat\partial f_i(x_i)\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), such that \(|f_i(x_i)-f_i(\bar x)|<\varepsilon\) for every \(i\) and \(\|x^*-\sum_{i=1}^m x_i^*\|<\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every Fréchet subgradient of a finite sum can be approximated arbitrarily closely by a sum of Fréchet subgradients evaluated at nearby points with nearby component-function values.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an Asplund space, and \(f_i:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), are lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\in\bigcap_i\operatorname{dom}f_i\).
All but at most one of the functions \(f_i\) are locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x^*\in\widehat\partial(\sum_{i=1}^m f_i)(\bar x)\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist points \(x_i\in B_\varepsilon(\bar x)\) and covectors \(x_i^*\in\widehat\partial f_i(x_i)\) such that \(|f_i(x_i)-f_i(\bar x)|<\varepsilon\) for every \(i\) and \(\|x^*-\sum_{i=1}^m x_i^*\|<\varepsilon\).

children.title: Fuzzy Chain Rules
children.top_down_role: Approximate subdifferential estimates for composite constructions.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are Asplund spaces, \(F:X\to Y\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\), and \(g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is lower semicontinuous near \(F(\bar x)\).
The composition \(g\circ F\) is finite at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x^*\in\widehat\partial(g\circ F)(\bar x)\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist \(x\in B_\varepsilon(\bar x)\), \(y\in B_\varepsilon(F(\bar x))\), and \(y^*\in\widehat\partial g(y)\) such that \(|g(y)-g(F(\bar x))|<\varepsilon\) and \(x^*\in\widehat D^*F(x)(y^*)+\varepsilon B_{X^*}\).

notation.meaning: Closed unit ball in the dual space

review_flags: exact fuzzy-chain hypotheses and proximity conditions require source confirmation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar composition rule stated in a fuzzy Fréchet-coderivative form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The fuzzy chain principle replaces an exact same-point formula by a nearby-point inclusion. Given \(x^*\in\widehat\partial(g\circ F)(\bar x)\) and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), suitable nearby points \(x\) and \(y\), together with \(y^*\in\widehat\partial g(y)\), yield \(x^*\in\widehat D^*F(x)(y^*)+\varepsilon B_{X^*}\), with \(y\) and its function value arbitrarily close to \(F(\bar x)\) and \(g(F(\bar x))\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subgradient of a composition is approximated by a nearby coderivative applied to a nearby outer subgradient.
knowledge_statements.title: Fuzzy Chain Rules

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an Asplund space.
The functions under consideration are lower semicontinuous, with the local Lipschitz assumptions required by the relevant finite-sum or composition rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fréchet subgradients of the combined function admit arbitrarily accurate decompositions through Fréchet subgradients or coderivatives evaluated at nearby points; the approximating points may be chosen to converge to the reference point with their function values converging accordingly.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In an Asplund space, the fuzzy variational principle supports approximate Fréchet-subdifferential calculus for lower semicontinuous data. Under the local Lipschitz hypotheses appropriate to the operation, each Fréchet subgradient of a sum or composition can be approximated arbitrarily closely by component Fréchet subgradients or coderivative images taken at nearby points, while preserving convergence of the associated function values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Asplund geometry supplies nearby-point Fréchet subgradient and coderivative decompositions for lower semicontinuous nonsmooth operations.

children.title: Exactness Recovery Regimes
children.top_down_role: Additional structure under which approximate rules strengthen toward exact calculus.

assumptions_latex: The relevant limiting subdifferential or coderivative is obtained by sequential outer limits of Fréchet constructions at nearby points.
A compactness condition permits extraction of convergent covector subsequences, and an appropriate singular qualification excludes nonzero abnormal limiting multipliers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Passing to the limit in the fuzzy inclusion yields an exact limiting-calculus inclusion at the reference point; equality requires additional structure, such as convexity with a continuity qualification or strict differentiability in the corresponding smooth operation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of reference-point limiting inclusions, and occasionally identities, from fuzzy calculus.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a fuzzy Fréchet rule produces nearby points and covectors for every tolerance tending to zero. If the covectors possess the compactness needed for convergent subsequences and the singular qualification eliminates abnormal limits, then the sequential definitions of limiting subgradients and coderivatives permit passage to an exact inclusion at the reference point. Exact equality is stronger and follows only under additional regularity appropriate to the operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compactness and exclusion of abnormal singular multipliers turn nearby-point fuzzy formulas into exact limiting inclusions; equality needs stronger regularity.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an Asplund space, \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is lower semicontinuous, and \(a,b\in X\) satisfy \([a,b]\subset\operatorname{dom}f\).
The number \(r\in\mathbb R\) satisfies \(r<f(b)-f(a)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist \(c\in[a,b)+\varepsilon B_X\) and \(c^*\in\widehat\partial f(c)\) such that \(|f(c)-f(a+t(b-a))|<\varepsilon\) for some \(t\in[0,1)\) and \(\langle c^*,b-a\rangle>r-\varepsilon\).

The point and function value can be chosen close to those of a point on the segment.

children.title: Exact Calculus Identities
children.top_down_role: Settings where generalized differential operations admit exact representations.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space and \(f,g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper lower semicontinuous convex functions.
There exists \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\) at which one summand is continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\), \(\partial(f+g)(x)=\partial f(x)+\partial g(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moreau-Rockafellar exact sum identity under a convex continuity qualification.

source_refs.locator: 3.2.1 Calculus Rules for Basic and Singular Subgradients p. 296
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated convex continuity qualification, the subdifferential sum rule is an identity rather than a one-sided estimate: \[\partial(f+g)(x)=\partial f(x)+\partial g(x).\] Thus every subgradient of the sum decomposes exactly into component subgradients at the same point, and every such component sum is a subgradient of \(f+g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For proper convex functions satisfying a continuity qualification, the subdifferential of their sum equals the sum of their subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Calculus Identities

children.title: Upper Calculus Estimates
children.top_down_role: One-sided generalized differential bounds lacking reverse containment.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an Asplund space, and \(f,g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\), with one summand locally Lipschitz there.
The singular qualification \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\cap[-\partial^\infty g(\bar x)]=\{0\}\) holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The limiting subdifferential satisfies \(\partial(f+g)(\bar x)\subset\partial f(\bar x)+\partial g(\bar x)\), and the singular subdifferential satisfies \(\partial^\infty(f+g)(\bar x)\subset\partial^\infty f(\bar x)+\partial^\infty g(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided limiting and singular subdifferential estimates for a finite sum.

source_refs.locator: 3.2.1 Calculus Rules for Basic and Singular Subgradients p. 296
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonsmooth nonconvex data, qualified calculus generally yields upper estimates rather than equality. At \(\bar x\), the limiting and singular subdifferentials obey \[\partial(f+g)(\bar x)\subset\partial f(\bar x)+\partial g(\bar x),\qquad \partial^\infty(f+g)(\bar x)\subset\partial^\infty f(\bar x)+\partial^\infty g(\bar x).\] Reverse inclusion need not hold without additional regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Qualified nonconvex subdifferential calculus usually gives an upper inclusion; the component sum may strictly exceed the subdifferential of the sum.
knowledge_statements.title: Upper Calculus Estimates

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2.1 Calculus Rules for Basic and Singular Subgradients p. 296

assumptions_latex: \(f,g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) are defined by \(f(x)=|x|\) and \(g(x)=-|x|\).
\(\partial\) denotes the Mordukhovich limiting subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \(0\), \(\partial(f+g)(0)=\{0\}\subsetneq\partial f(0)+\partial g(0)=[-2,2]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional strictness example for the limiting-subdifferential upper sum rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=|x|\) and \(g(x)=-|x|\), \(f+g\equiv0\), while \(\partial f(0)=[-1,1]\) and \(\partial g(0)=\{-1,1\}\). Hence \(\partial(f+g)(0)=\{0\}\subsetneq\partial f(0)+\partial g(0)=[-2,2]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For absolute value plus negative absolute value, the sum is identically zero but the sum of the limiting subdifferentials at zero is the interval from minus two to two, so the upper inclusion is strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strictness of the Limiting Sum Estimate

knowledge_statements.title: Fuzzy Calculus Inclusions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nearby-point inclusion representing the fuzzy level of the exactness hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\varepsilon>0\) and every \(x^*\in\widehat\partial(\sum_i f_i)(\bar x)\), there exist points \(x_i\in B_\varepsilon(\bar x)\) such that \(|f_i(x_i)-f_i(\bar x)|<\varepsilon\) for every \(i\) and \[x^*\in\sum_i\widehat\partial f_i(x_i)+\varepsilon B_{X^*}.\] Thus both the component evaluation points and the resulting covector sum may differ from their exact reference-point counterparts by arbitrarily small amounts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each selected Fréchet subgradient of the sum admits a nearby-point component decomposition with an arbitrarily small dual-space error.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an Asplund space, \(f_i:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\), and all but at most one are locally Lipschitz there.
A tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(x^*\in\widehat\partial(\sum_i f_i)(\bar x)\) are fixed.

knowledge_statements.title: Exactness Qualification Thresholds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: No-abnormal-cancellation qualification used when deriving exact limiting inclusions from fuzzy calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A standard qualification for a finite family excludes nontrivial singular cancellation: \[x_i^*\in\partial^\infty f_i(\bar x),\quad \sum_i x_i^*=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x_1^*=\cdots=x_m^*=0.\] For two functions this condition is equivalent to \[\partial^\infty f_1(\bar x)\cap[-\partial^\infty f_2(\bar x)]=\{0\}.\] Analogous mapping qualifications use zero-input coderivative images. Additional compactness or sequential-normal-compactness assumptions may be required in infinite-dimensional limiting calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A standard exact-calculus qualification rules out nontrivial cancellation among singular subgradients or zero-input coderivative elements; infinite-dimensional results may require additional compactness assumptions.
assumptions_latex: A candidate exact limiting-calculus rule is obtained by passing to the limit in a fuzzy Fréchet rule.
The relevant singular objects are \(\partial^\infty f_i(\bar x)\), or the corresponding zero-input coderivative images for mapping rules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The no-abnormal-cancellation condition is \(x_i^*\in\partial^\infty f_i(\bar x)\) and \(\sum_i x_i^*=0\Rightarrow x_i^*=0\) for every \(i\). For two functions it becomes \(\partial^\infty f_1(\bar x)\cap[-\partial^\infty f_2(\bar x)]=\{0\}\).

children.title: Coderivative Sum Calculus
children.top_down_role: Coderivative behavior for additive combinations of mappings.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional limiting-coderivative estimate for a multifunction sum with decomposition compactness and explicit abnormal-multiplier exclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x):=\sum_{i=1}^mF_i(x)\) and define the decomposition mapping
\[
\Xi(x,y):=\{(y_1,\ldots,y_m):y_i\in F_i(x),\ \sum_i y_i=y\}.
\]
Assume \(\Xi\) is inner semicompact at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) relative to its domain. Suppose that, for every \((\bar y_1,\ldots,\bar y_m)\in\Xi(\bar x,\bar y)\),
\[
x_i^*\in D^*F_i(\bar x,\bar y_i)(0),\quad \sum_i x_i^*=0
\Longrightarrow x_i^*=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).
\]
Then, for every \(y^*\in Y^*\),
\[
D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)
\subset
\bigcup_{(\bar y_1,\ldots,\bar y_m)\in\Xi(\bar x,\bar y)}
\sum_{i=1}^mD^*F_i(\bar x,\bar y_i)(y^*).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With compact control of nearby output decompositions and no cancelling horizontal abnormal multipliers, a sum coderivative is assembled from component coderivatives sharing the same output covector.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional normed spaces and the component graphs are locally closed near every relevant decomposition.
The decomposition mapping \(\Xi\) is inner semicompact at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) relative to its domain.
The displayed horizontal abnormal-multiplier condition holds at every reference decomposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\subset\bigcup_{\Xi(\bar x,\bar y)}\sum_iD^*F_i(\bar x,\bar y_i)(y^*)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Coderivative Sum Rule

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are Asplund spaces, and \(F_i:X\rightrightarrows Y\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), have locally closed graphs near \((\bar x,\bar y_i)\).
The sum mapping is \(F(x):=\sum_iF_i(x)\), with \(\bar y=\sum_i\bar y_i\), and the relevant coderivative normal qualification holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(y^*\in Y^*\), \(D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\subset\bigcup_{\sum_i y_i=\bar y,\ y_i\in F_i(\bar x)}\sum_iD^*F_i(\bar x,y_i)(y^*)\).
review_flags: precise normal qualification should be matched to the cited theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualified limiting-coderivative upper estimate for a finite Minkowski sum.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F:=\sum_iF_i\), every limiting coderivative element at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is bounded above by component coderivatives associated with a decomposition of \(\bar y\): \[D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\subset\bigcup_{\substack{y_i\in F_i(\bar x)\\\sum_i y_i=\bar y}}\sum_iD^*F_i(\bar x,y_i)(y^*).\] The same dual argument \(y^*\) enters every component because output addition is linear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The coderivative of a multifunction sum is contained in sums of component coderivatives over all compatible decompositions of the output.

children.title: Coderivative Product Calculus
children.top_down_role: Coderivative behavior for Cartesian products of mappings or graphs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional limiting-coderivative estimate for a common-input Cartesian product mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
P(x):=F_1(x)\times\cdots\times F_m(x),\qquad \bar y=(\bar y_1,\ldots,\bar y_m).
\]
Assume the component graphs are locally closed and
\[
x_i^*\in D^*F_i(\bar x,\bar y_i)(0),\quad \sum_{i=1}^m x_i^*=0
\Longrightarrow x_i^*=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).
\]
Then, for every \((y_1^*,\ldots,y_m^*)\),
\[
D^*P(\bar x,\bar y)(y_1^*,\ldots,y_m^*)
\subset
\sum_{i=1}^mD^*F_i(\bar x,\bar y_i)(y_i^*).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under horizontal abnormal-multiplier exclusion, each output covector acts on its corresponding component and the resulting input covectors add.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y_i\) are finite-dimensional normed spaces.
Each \(F_i\) has locally closed graph at \((\bar x,\bar y_i)\).
No nonzero horizontal component coderivatives cancel as displayed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D^*P(\bar x,\bar y)(y_1^*,\ldots,y_m^*)\subset\sum_iD^*F_i(\bar x,\bar y_i)(y_i^*)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Coderivative Product Rule

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y_i\) are Asplund spaces, and \(F_i:X\rightrightarrows Y_i\) have locally closed graphs near \((\bar x,\bar y_i)\).
The product mapping is \(F(x):=F_1(x)\times\cdots\times F_m(x)\), and the component graphs satisfy the relevant normal qualification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(y^*=(y_1^*,\ldots,y_m^*)\), \(D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\subset\sum_{i=1}^mD^*F_i(\bar x,\bar y_i)(y_i^*)\).

children.title: Coderivative Intersection Calculus
children.top_down_role: Coderivative behavior for graph intersections and coupled constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional limiting-coderivative estimate for a pointwise intersection under explicit graph-normal transversality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x):=\bigcap_{i=1}^mF_i(x)\), with \(\bar y\in F_i(\bar x)\) for every \(i\). Assume the graphs are locally closed and
\[
\left.\begin{array}{c}
x_i^*\in D^*F_i(\bar x,\bar y)(y_i^*),\quad i=1,\ldots,m,\\
\sum_i x_i^*=0,\qquad \sum_i y_i^*=0
\end{array}\right\}
\Longrightarrow (x_i^*,y_i^*)=(0,0)\ \text{for every }i.
\]
Then, for every \(y^*\in Y^*\),
\[
D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)
\subset
\bigcup_{\sum_i y_i^*=y^*}
\sum_{i=1}^mD^*F_i(\bar x,\bar y)(y_i^*).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under graph-normal transversality, a coderivative of a pointwise intersection decomposes into component coderivatives whose output covectors sum to the prescribed covector.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional normed spaces.
Each \(F_i\) has locally closed graph at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
The displayed full graph-normal cancellation condition holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\subset\bigcup_{\sum_i y_i^*=y^*}\sum_iD^*F_i(\bar x,\bar y)(y_i^*)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Coderivative Intersection Rule

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are Asplund spaces, and \(F_i:X\rightrightarrows Y\) have locally closed graphs near \((\bar x,\bar y)\), where \(\bar y\in\bigcap_iF_i(\bar x)\).
The intersection mapping is \(F(x):=\bigcap_iF_i(x)\), and the component graphs satisfy the relevant normal qualification.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the pointwise intersection \(F:=\bigcap_iF_i\), qualified normal-cone calculus gives \[D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\subset\bigcup_{\sum_i y_i^*=y^*}\sum_{i=1}^mD^*F_i(\bar x,\bar y)(y_i^*).\] Unlike output addition, intersection requires the output covector \(y^*\) to be decomposed among the active component graphs.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The multioperation coderivative qualification at \((\bar x,\bar y_1,\ldots,\bar y_m)\) is
\[
\left.
\begin{array}{c}
x_i^*\in D^*F_i(\bar x,\bar y_i)(0),\quad i=1,\ldots,m,\\
\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^m x_i^*=0
\end{array}
\right\}
\Longrightarrow x_1^*=\cdots=x_m^*=0.
\]
It excludes nonzero collections of horizontal coderivative multipliers whose domain components cancel, thereby furnishing the normal-cone qualification used in product, sum, and intersection coderivative calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: No nonzero collection of horizontal coderivative multipliers may cancel across mappings sharing the same input.
knowledge_statements.title: Multioperation Coderivative Qualifications

children.title: Coderivative Composition Calculus
children.top_down_role: Coderivative calculus for composed set-valued mappings.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y,Z\) are finite-dimensional normed spaces.
\(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) and \(G:Y\rightrightarrows Z\) have locally closed graphs near every \((\bar x,y)\) and \((y,\bar z)\), respectively, with \(y\in\mathcal M(\bar x,\bar z)\).
The intermediate-point mapping \(\mathcal M(x,z):=F(x)\cap G^{-1}(z)\) is inner semicompact at \((\bar x,\bar z)\) relative to its domain.
For every \(y\in\mathcal M(\bar x,\bar z)\), \(D^*G(y,\bar z)(0)\cap\ker D^*F(\bar x,y)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(z^*\in Z^*\), the limiting coderivative of \(G\circ F\) satisfies the displayed chain-rule inclusion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional limiting-coderivative chain rule with inner-semicompact localization of intermediate points.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.2 Calculus of Coderivatives p. 274

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\bar x,\bar z)\in\operatorname{gph}(G\circ F)\). Then, for every \(z^*\in Z^*\),
\[
D^*(G\circ F)(\bar x,\bar z)(z^*)
\subset
\bigcup_{y\in\mathcal M(\bar x,\bar z)}
\bigcup_{y^*\in D^*G(y,\bar z)(z^*)}
D^*F(\bar x,y)(y^*).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the intermediate-point mapping is inner semicompact and the coderivative abnormal-multiplier condition holds at every relevant intermediate point, the coderivative of the composition satisfies the chain-rule inclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Coderivative Composition Calculus

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Because \(\operatorname{gph}F^{-1}\) is obtained from \(\operatorname{gph}F\) by exchanging coordinates, for every \(x^*\in X^*\),
\[
D^*F^{-1}(\bar y,\bar x)(x^*)
=
\{y^*\in Y^*:-x^*\in D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(-y^*)\}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
y^*\in D^*F^{-1}(\bar y,\bar x)(x^*)
\Longleftrightarrow
(-x^*,y^*)\in N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inverse-mapping coderivative is the original coderivative with domain and range exchanged and both dual arguments sign-adjusted.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(K\) is inner semicompact at \((\bar x,\bar z)\) relative to \(\operatorname{dom}K\) if, for every sequence
\[
(x_k,z_k)\to(\bar x,\bar z),
\qquad (x_k,z_k)\in\operatorname{dom}K,
\]
there exist selections \(y_k\in K(x_k,z_k)\) and a subsequence \(\{y_{k_j}\}\) converging in \(Y\). If \(\operatorname{gph}K\) is locally closed at the resulting limit point, then that limit belongs to \(K(\bar x,\bar z)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every feasible parameter sequence approaching the reference point admits selections with a convergent subsequence; membership of the limit in the reference value additionally follows from local graph closedness.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) given by \(F(x)=x^2\), one has
\[
D^*F(0,0)(y^*)=\{0\}\quad\text{for every }y^*\in\mathbb R,
\]
so
\[
\{y^*:0\in D^*F(0,0)(y^*)\}=\mathbb R\neq\{0\}.
\]
The inverse satisfies \(F^{-1}(y)=\{-\sqrt y,\sqrt y\}\) for \(y>0\), and its branches are not Lipschitz at \(0\). Equivalently, the implicit equation \(x^2-y=0\) has no Aubin-stable solution localization at \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The square map has a fully degenerate coderivative at zero, and its square-root inverse branches are not Lipschitz there.
knowledge_statements.title: Inverse–Implicit Degeneracy Boundaries

source_refs.locator: 3.1 Calculus Rules for Normals and Coderivatives p. 261

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the tangent-intersection hypothesis, for every \(u\in X\),
\[
DP(\bar x,(\bar y_1,\ldots,\bar y_m))(u)
=
DF_1(\bar x,\bar y_1)(u)\times\cdots\times DF_m(\bar x,\bar y_m)(u).
\]
For any set-valued mapping \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), coordinate exchange of its graph gives the unconditional inverse formula
\[
DF^{-1}(\bar y,\bar x)(v)
=
\{u\in X:v\in DF(\bar x,\bar y)(u)\}.
\]
Both identities follow directly from the corresponding contingent-tangent representations of the operation graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under tangent compatibility, graphical derivatives commute with common-input products; inversion always exchanges the derivative input and output directions.
knowledge_statements.title: Graphical-Derivative Operation Calculus

source_witnesses.locator: 3.1 Calculus Rules for Normals and Coderivatives p. 261
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contingent sum rule separating synchronized inner inclusion from exact tangent decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H(x):=\sum_{i=1}^mF_i(x)\) and \(\bar y=\sum_i\bar y_i\), with \(\bar y_i\in F_i(\bar x)\). If component tangent arcs for a common direction \(u\) can be synchronized, then
\[
\sum_{i=1}^mDF_i(\bar x,\bar y_i)(u)\subset DH(\bar x,\bar y)(u).
\]
If, in addition, every tangent to \(\operatorname{gph}H\) lifts to a compatible value decomposition and all such component tangents are synchronizable, then
\[
DH(\bar x,\bar y)(u)=\bigcup_{\substack{\bar y_i\in F_i(\bar x)\\\sum_i\bar y_i=\bar y}}\sum_{i=1}^mDF_i(\bar x,\bar y_i)(u).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Synchronized component tangents add to a sum tangent; equality requires every sum tangent to lift to a compatible component decomposition.
assumptions_latex: \(F_i:X\rightrightarrows Y\) act between finite-dimensional spaces.
The inner inclusion uses synchronized component tangent arcs.
The equality additionally uses exhaustive tangent lifting over compatible reference-value decompositions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inner inclusion holds under synchronization and becomes equality under two-sided tangent decomposition.
knowledge_statements.title: Graphical-Derivative Sum Rule

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact contingent chain representation under explicit two-sided tangent lifting through intermediate points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H:=G\circ F\) and \(K(x,z):=F(x)\cap G^{-1}(z)\). Suppose every tangent to \(\operatorname{gph}H\) at \((\bar x,\bar z)\) lifts through some \(\bar y\in K(\bar x,\bar z)\), and every compatible pair \((u,v)\in T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\), \((v,w)\in T_{\operatorname{gph}G}(\bar y,\bar z)\) is realizable by synchronized graph arcs of the composition. Then
\[
DH(\bar x,\bar z)(u)=\bigcup_{\bar y\in K(\bar x,\bar z)}\ \bigcup_{v\in DF(\bar x,\bar y)(u)}DG(\bar y,\bar z)(v).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When composition tangents lift and component tangent arcs can be synchronized, graphical derivatives propagate directions successively through the two mappings.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) and \(G:Y\rightrightarrows Z\) act between finite-dimensional spaces.
The stated two-sided tangent-lifting and synchronization property holds at \((\bar x,\bar z)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(DH(\bar x,\bar z)(u)=\bigcup_{\bar y\in K(\bar x,\bar z)}\bigcup_{v\in DF(\bar x,\bar y)(u)}DG(\bar y,\bar z)(v)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Graphical-Derivative Composition Rule

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed space.
\(f_1,f_2:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\), with \(f_1(\bar x)\) and \(f_2(\bar x)\) finite.

source_refs.locator: 3.2.1 Calculus Rules for Basic and Singular Subgradients p. 296
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The singular-subgradient qualification for addition is
\[
\partial^\infty f_1(\bar x)\cap\bigl(-\partial^\infty f_2(\bar x)\bigr)=\{0\}.
\]
Equivalently, if \(x_1^*\in\partial^\infty f_1(\bar x)\), \(x_2^*\in\partial^\infty f_2(\bar x)\), and \(x_1^*+x_2^*=0\), then \(x_1^*=x_2^*=0\). Under this qualification,
\[
\partial(f_1+f_2)(\bar x)
\subset
\partial f_1(\bar x)+\partial f_2(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Opposing nonzero singular subgradients are excluded; for lower-semicontinuous functions in finite dimensions, this yields the limiting-subdifferential sum inclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular-Subgradient Qualifications

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2.1 Calculus Rules for Basic and Singular Subgradients p. 296
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-family extension of the limiting-subdifferential sum qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\) and finite at \(\bar x\), with \(X\) finite-dimensional. If \[x_i^*\in\partial^\infty f_i(\bar x)\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m x_i^*=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x_1^*=\cdots=x_m^*=0,\] then \[\partial\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\right)(\bar x)\subseteq\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(\bar x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite sum, exclusion of every nontrivial balanced tuple of singular subgradients yields the limiting-subdifferential sum inclusion.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional.
Each \(f_i\) is lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\) and finite at \(\bar x\).
The singular no-balancing condition holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(\sum_{i=1}^m f_i)(\bar x)\subseteq\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(\bar x).\)
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sum Singular Qualification

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Automatic finite-sum singular qualification when all but at most one summand are locally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz around \(\bar x\), then \[\partial^\infty f(\bar x)=\{0\}.\] Consequently, the finite-sum singular no-balancing qualification holds automatically whenever all but at most one summand are locally Lipschitz around \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local Lipschitzness annihilates the singular subdifferential, so a finite sum is automatically singularly qualified when at most one summand is non-Lipschitz.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional.
All but at most one of \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\) are locally Lipschitz around \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^\infty f_i(\bar x)=\{0\}\) for every locally Lipschitz summand, and the finite-sum singular qualification holds automatically.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Lipschitz Sufficient Regime

children.title: Normal-Cone Transversality
children.top_down_role: Geometric opposition conditions for intersections and inverse images.

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega_1,\Omega_2\) are locally closed subsets of a finite-dimensional normed space.
\(\bar x\in\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Transversality yields the limiting-normal intersection inclusion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional normal-cone opposition condition for intersections; inverse-image qualifications follow by applying it to lifted graph sets.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.1 Calculus of Normal Cones p. 262
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The sets \(\Omega_1\) and \(\Omega_2\) are normally transversal at \(\bar x\) when
\[
N_{\Omega_1}(\bar x)\cap\bigl(-N_{\Omega_2}(\bar x)\bigr)=\{0\}.
\]
Under this condition, the limiting normal cone to their intersection satisfies
\[
N_{\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2}(\bar x)
\subset
N_{\Omega_1}(\bar x)+N_{\Omega_2}(\bar x).
\]
The same condition applied to graph and constraint sets supplies the geometric qualification for inverse-image and generalized-equation calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two sets are transversal when their limiting normals cannot oppose nontrivially; then intersection normals decompose into normals to the individual sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Transversality

source_witnesses.locator: 3.1.1 Calculus of Normal Cones p. 262
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-family extension of the two-set normal-cone qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_m\) be locally closed subsets of a finite-dimensional normed space and let \(\bar x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^m\Omega_i\). If \[x_i^*\in N_{\Omega_i}(\bar x)\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m x_i^*=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x_1^*=\cdots=x_m^*=0,\] then \[N_{\cap_{i=1}^m\Omega_i}(\bar x)\subseteq\sum_{i=1}^mN_{\Omega_i}(\bar x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite set family is normally transversal when no nontrivial selection of limiting normals balances to zero; then intersection normals decompose into component normals.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_m\) are locally closed in a finite-dimensional normed space.
\(\bar x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^m\Omega_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\cap_i\Omega_i}(\bar x)\subseteq\sum_iN_{\Omega_i}(\bar x)\) under the no-balancing condition.

notation.meaning: limiting normal cone to the ith set

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Family Normal Transversality

children.title: Metric-Regularity Qualifications
children.top_down_role: Metric stability regimes supporting generalized differential calculus.

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has locally closed graph near \((\bar x,\bar y)\) in finite-dimensional spaces.
\((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed coderivative-kernel condition is equivalent to metric regularity around \((\bar x,\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: distance from a point to a set

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is metrically regular around \((\bar x,\bar y)\) precisely when there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\), \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and \(\kappa>0\) such that
\[
d(x,F^{-1}(y))\leq\kappa d(y,F(x))
\quad\text{for all }(x,y)\in U\times V,
\]
and this is equivalent to the coderivative qualification
\[
0\in D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)
\Longrightarrow y^*=0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric regularity is equivalent, in finite dimensions, to the absence of nonzero dual vectors mapped to zero by the coderivative.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Regularity Qualifications

children.title: Normal-Compactness Qualifications
children.top_down_role: Sequential compactness regimes controlling limiting normal behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an Asplund space and \(\Omega\subset X\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\).
Normals in the sequential test are Fréchet normals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed implication defines sequential normal compactness at \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: weak-star convergence in the dual space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential normal compactness for sets in Asplund spaces; it is automatic in finite dimensions.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.4 Sequential Normal Compactness of Sets p. 27
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The set \(\Omega\) is sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\in\Omega\) if every pair of sequences satisfying
\[
x_k\xrightarrow{\Omega}\bar x,
\qquad x_k^*\in\widehat N_\Omega(x_k),
\qquad x_k^*\xrightarrow{w^*}0
\]
also satisfies
\[
\|x_k^*\|\to0.
\]
Thus weak-star disappearance of nearby Fréchet normals cannot occur while their norms remain bounded away from zero. In finite-dimensional spaces, weak-star and norm convergence coincide, so this property holds automatically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential normal compactness requires weak-star vanishing nearby Fréchet normals to vanish in norm; finite-dimensional sets satisfy it automatically.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Compactness Qualifications

children.title: Metric–Compactness Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Interactions between metric stability and normal compactness assumptions.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is Asplund, and \(\Omega_1,\Omega_2\subset X\) are locally closed at \(\bar x\in\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2\).
At least one set is sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\).
The limiting-normal transversality condition holds at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The intersection is sequentially normally compact and obeys the limiting-normal sum inclusion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility of normal transversality and sequential compactness in Asplund-space intersection calculus.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Sequential Normal Compactness of Set Intersections and Inverse Images p. 341
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose
\[
N_{\Omega_1}(\bar x)\cap\bigl(-N_{\Omega_2}(\bar x)\bigr)=\{0\},
\]
and at least one of \(\Omega_1\) and \(\Omega_2\) is sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\). Then \(\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2\) is sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\), and
\[
N_{\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2}(\bar x)
\subset
N_{\Omega_1}(\bar x)+N_{\Omega_2}(\bar x).
\]
Transversality removes abnormal cancellation, while normal compactness prevents nonvanishing multiplier mass from disappearing only in the weak-star topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normal transversality and sequential normal compactness together preserve compactness and yield the limiting-normal intersection rule.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric–Compactness Compatibility

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional metric interpretation of the normal qualification used in compactness-supported intersection calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega_1,\Omega_2\subset X\) be locally closed near \(\bar x\in\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2\), where \(X\) is finite-dimensional, and define \[\Phi(x):=(\Omega_1-x)\times(\Omega_2-x).\] Then \(\Phi\) is metrically regular around \((\bar x,(0,0))\) if and only if \[N_{\Omega_1}(\bar x)\cap\bigl(-N_{\Omega_2}(\bar x)\bigr)=\{0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two locally closed finite-dimensional sets, normal transversality is equivalent to metric regularity of the lifted mapping encoding their intersection.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional.
\(\Omega_1\) and \(\Omega_2\) are locally closed near \(\bar x\in\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2\).
\(\Phi(x)=(\Omega_1-x)\times(\Omega_2-x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi\text{ is metrically regular around }(\bar x,(0,0))\iff N_{\Omega_1}(\bar x)\cap[-N_{\Omega_2}(\bar x)]=\{0\}.\)

children.top_down_role: Calculus losses caused by failure of metric or compactness support.

assumptions_latex: \(f,g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper and lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\cap[-\partial^\infty g(\bar x)]\ne\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: Mordukhovich singular subdifferential of f at x

review_flags: Failure of the qualification does not itself assert failure of every calculus conclusion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the standard singular-subgradient qualification for a limiting sum rule.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The singular-subgradient qualification for the limiting sum rule fails at \(\bar x\) precisely when
\[\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\cap[-\partial^\infty g(\bar x)]\ne\{0\}.\]
Equivalently, there is a nonzero \(v\) with \(v\in\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\) and \(-v\in\partial^\infty g(\bar x)\). In this regime the usual qualification-based derivation of \(\partial(f+g)(\bar x)\subset\partial f(\bar x)+\partial g(\bar x)\) is unavailable; the condition alone does not imply that the inclusion is false.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Qualification fails when the summands possess nonzero opposite singular subgradients. The standard sum-rule theorem then becomes inapplicable, although its conclusion may still hold accidentally.
knowledge_statements.title: Qualification Failure Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact sequential failure boundary for the compactness component of the parent qualification architecture.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A locally closed set \(\Omega\subset X\) fails to be sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\in\Omega\) exactly when there exist sequences \[x_k\xrightarrow{\Omega}\bar x,\qquad x_k^*\in\widehat N_\Omega(x_k),\qquad x_k^*\xrightarrow{w^*}0,\] for which \(\|x_k^*\|\not\to0\). After passage to a subsequence and positive normalization, the witness can be chosen with \(\|x_k^*\|=1\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SNC fails precisely when nearby Fréchet normals vanish weak-star without vanishing in norm; unit-norm witnesses can be used.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset X\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\in\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Omega\text{ is not SNC at }\bar x\iff\exists x_k\to_\Omega\bar x,\ x_k^*\in\widehat N_\Omega(x_k),\ x_k^*\xrightarrow{w^*}0,\ \|x_k^*\|\not\to0.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Normal-Compactness Failure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional failure boundary for the metric component of the parent qualification architecture.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) have locally closed graph near \((\bar x,\bar y)\) in finite-dimensional spaces. The metric-regularity qualification fails exactly when \[\ker D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)\ne\{0\},\] equivalently, when some \(y^*\ne0\) satisfies \[0\in D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, the metric qualification fails exactly when a nonzero output covector is mapped to zero by the coderivative.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has locally closed graph near \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
\(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is not metrically regular around }(\bar x,\bar y)\iff\ker D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)\ne\{0\}.\)

source_refs.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the Mordukhovich limiting subdifferential, local Lipschitz continuity of one summand removes its nonzero singular subgradients and yields the one-sided estimate
\[\partial(f+g)(\bar x)\subseteq\partial f(\bar x)+\partial g(\bar x).\]
This statement is only an upper calculus inclusion: it does not assert that every vector formed by adding a member of \(\partial f(\bar x)\) to a member of \(\partial g(\bar x)\) belongs to \(\partial(f+g)(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With one summand locally Lipschitz, every limiting subgradient of the sum decomposes into subgradients of the summands; the reverse inclusion need not hold.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Calculus Inclusions

children.title: Equality Recovery Regimes
children.top_down_role: Additional structure restoring equality from one-sided estimates.

assumptions_latex: \(f,g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
\(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(f+g)(x)=\partial f(x)+\partial g(x)\) for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex exact sum rule under relative-interior qualification.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If the relative interiors of the effective domains meet, then for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\) the convex subdifferential satisfies the exact sum rule
\[\partial(f+g)(x)=\partial f(x)+\partial g(x).\]
Thus both the upper calculus inclusion and its reverse hold. In finite dimensions the convex and Mordukhovich limiting subdifferentials coincide for proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions, so the equality also supplies an equality-recovery regime for limiting calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For proper closed convex functions whose domain relative interiors intersect, the subdifferential of their sum equals the Minkowski sum of their subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.title: Equality Recovery Regimes

source_refs.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At the origin, \(f+g\equiv0\), while
\[\partial f(0)=[-1,1],\qquad \partial g(0)=\{-1,1\}.\]
Consequently,
\[\partial(f+g)(0)=\{0\}\subsetneq[-2,2]=\partial f(0)+\partial g(0).\]
Both functions are locally Lipschitz, so the applicable one-sided sum estimate can be strictly larger than the true limiting subdifferential even when its qualification is satisfied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The functions absolute value and minus absolute value sum to zero, but the sum of their limiting subdifferentials strictly overestimates the exact subdifferential.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An upper calculus estimate \(\partial F(\bar x)\subseteq E(\bar x)\) is vacuous at \(\bar x\) when
\[E(\bar x)=\mathbb{R}^n.\]
The displayed inclusion then reduces to the ambient fact \(\partial F(\bar x)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and excludes no candidate subgradient. More generally, vacuity relative to a prescribed admissible set \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) means \(E(\bar x)\supseteq A\), so the estimate supplies no restriction beyond prior admissibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A calculus upper bound is vacuous when it equals the entire ambient dual space, and therefore rules out no possible subgradient.
knowledge_statements.title: Vacuous Estimate Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The second directional derivative of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) in direction \(h\) is the finite limit
\[f''(\bar x;h):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(\bar x+th)-f(\bar x)-t f'(\bar x;h)}{\tfrac12t^2},\]

For each \(w\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the second subderivative of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) relative to \(\bar v\) is
\[d^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w):=\liminf_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\w'\to w}}\frac{f(\bar x+t w')-f(\bar x)-t\langle\bar v,w'\rangle}{\tfrac12t^2}.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second subderivative is the lower quadratic growth after subtracting a reference linear form, allowing nearby directions as the step tends to zero.

The basic second-order subdifferential of \(f\) at \((\bar x,\bar v)\) is the coderivative of its limiting-subdifferential mapping:
\[\partial^2f(\bar x,\bar v)(u):=D^*(\partial f)(\bar x,\bar v)(u)=\left\{w\in\mathbb{R}^n:(w,-u)\in N_{\operatorname{gph}\partial f}(\bar x,\bar v)\right\}.\]

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are Asplund spaces, \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The regular coderivative uses the Fréchet normal at the reference graph point. The mixed coderivative permits graph-point approximation, requires \(u_k\to u\) in norm, and permits \(x_k^{*}\overset{w^{*}}{\longrightarrow}x^{*}\). The limiting coderivative permits weak-star convergence for both dual components in its normal approximation. Consequently, for every \(u\in Y^{*}\), \[\widehat D^{*}F(\bar x,\bar y)(u)\subset D_M^{*}F(\bar x,\bar y)(u)\subset D^{*}F(\bar x,\bar y)(u).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated conventions, stronger convergence requirements yield the nesting regular coderivative contained in mixed coderivative contained in limiting coderivative.
knowledge_statements.title: Convergence-Sensitive Regimes

If \(f\) is twice continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\) and \(\bar v=\nabla f(\bar x)\), then all three variants coincide and satisfy \[\breve\partial^{2}f(\bar x,\bar v)(u)=\partial_M^{2}f(\bar x,\bar v)(u)=\partial^{2}f(\bar x,\bar v)(u)=\{\nabla^{2}f(\bar x)u\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The variants are nested and coincide for smooth functions; nonsmooth graph irregularity can make either inclusion strict.

children.title: Partial Second-Order Subdifferentials
children.top_down_role: Second-order constructions for parameterized and block-structured functions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar smooth example separating projection of the full response from a zero-parameter-covector restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x,p)=xp\), one has \(S(x,p)=\partial_xf(x,p)=\{p\}\) and \[D^*S((0,0),0)(u)=\{(0,u)\}.\] Hence the decision-coordinate projection is \(\{0\}\) for every \(u\), whereas \(\{w:(w,0)\in D^*S((0,0),0)(u)\}\) is empty whenever \(u\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even for a smooth coupled function, projecting the full coderivative output differs from requiring the parameter component to vanish.
assumptions_latex: \(X=P=\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(u\ne0\), \(\operatorname{proj}_X D^*S((0,0),0)(u)=\{0\}\) but \(\{w:(w,0)\in D^*S((0,0),0)(u)\}=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Projection–Zero-Slice Separation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full Coderivative Response of a Partial Subgradient Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Treats the coderivative's full product-space output as primary; coordinate projections and zero-coordinate slices are distinct derived constructions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S(x,p):=\partial_x f(x,p)\). For \(u\in X\), define the full partial second-order response by \[\mathcal H_x f((\bar x,\bar p),\bar v)(u):=D^*S((\bar x,\bar p),\bar v)(u)\subset X\times P.\] Its decision and parameter responses are the coordinate projections of this set. Requiring an output of the form \((w,0)\) is a separate zero-parameter-covector slice and is not generally equivalent to projecting onto the decision coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The coderivative of the partial subgradient mapping has a full product-space output; coordinate projections must not be confused with imposing a zero value in another coordinate.
assumptions_latex: \(X,P\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
\(f:X\times P\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(\bar v\in\partial_x f(\bar x,\bar p)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D^*(\partial_x f)((\bar x,\bar p),\bar v)(u)\subset X\times P\), with projections and zero-coordinate slices constituting distinct derived objects.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The subgradient mapping is proto-differentiable at \((\bar x,\bar v)\) when the difference-quotient mappings \[Q_t(u):=\frac{\partial f(\bar x+tu)-\bar v}{t}\] converge graphically as \(t\downarrow0\). Their graphical limit is the proto-derivative, equivalently the graphical derivative, and satisfies \[D(\partial f)(\bar x,\bar v)(u)=\{z\in X:(u,z)\in T_{\operatorname{gph}\partial f}(\bar x,\bar v)\}.\] Thus it records all first-order tangent variations of subgradients generated by a primal direction \(u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subgradient proto-derivative consists of tangent subgradient variations associated with a prescribed primal direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient Proto-Derivatives

children.title: Twice Epi-Differentiability
children.top_down_role: Stable second-order epigraphical approximation and its mapping consequences.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates existence of an epi-limit from the additional requirement that the limit be proper.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(t>0\), set \[\Delta_t^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w):=\frac{f(\bar x+tw)-f(\bar x)-t\langle\bar v,w\rangle}{\tfrac12t^2}.\] The function is twice epi-differentiable at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) when \(\Delta_t^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\) epi-converges as \(t\downarrow0\); its epi-limit is \(d_e^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\). It is properly twice epi-differentiable when this epi-limit is additionally a proper extended-real function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Twice epi-differentiability requires an epi-limit of normalized second-order quotients; proper twice epi-differentiability additionally requires that limit to be proper.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(\bar v\in\partial f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ordinary twice epi-differentiability asserts epi-convergence; proper twice epi-differentiability adds properness of \(d_e^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Ordinary and Proper Twice Epi-Differentiability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex correspondence under the one-half squared-step normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper lower semicontinuous convex function, proper twice epi-differentiability of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) is equivalent to proto-differentiability of \(\partial f\) at \((\bar x,\bar v)\). In that case, \[D(\partial f)(\bar x,\bar v)(w)=\partial\!\left(\tfrac12d_e^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\right)(w)\qquad(w\in X).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex function, proper twice epi-differentiability is equivalent to proto-differentiability of the subgradient mapping, with the proto-derivative represented by the subdifferential of half the second epi-derivative.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
\((\bar x,\bar v)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(\partial f)(\bar x,\bar v)=\partial(\tfrac12d_e^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v))\) whenever the equivalent proper twice-epi/proto-differentiability conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Proto-Derivative Correspondence

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous, with \(\bar v\in\partial f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is twice epi-differentiable at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) exactly when \(\Delta_t^{2}f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\) epi-converges as \(t\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the normalization with denominator one-half times the squared step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(t>0\), define the second-order difference quotient by \[\Delta_t^{2}f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w):=\frac{f(\bar x+tw)-f(\bar x)-t\langle\bar v,w\rangle}{\tfrac12 t^{2}}.\] The function \(f\) is twice epi-differentiable at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) if these functions epi-converge as \(t\downarrow0\). The resulting proper extended-real function, when it exists, is \[d_e^{2}f(\bar x\mid\bar v):=\operatorname{e-lim}_{t\downarrow0}\Delta_t^{2}f(\bar x\mid\bar v).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Twice epi-differentiability means that normalized second-order difference quotients have a well-defined epigraphical limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Twice Epi-Differentiability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normalization and epi-convergence formulation are recognizable standard definitions, but the record has no citation. Moreover, calling the resulting epi-limit proper may require the stronger notion of proper twice epi-differentiability rather than twice epi-differentiability alone. An authoritative definition with an exact locator is required before choosing the correct formulation.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The smooth perturbation identity \[\partial(f+g)(x)=\partial f(x)+\nabla g(x)\] induces an exact graph transformation of the subgradient mapping. Consequently, for every direction \(u\in\mathbb R^{n}\), \[\partial^{2}(f+g)(\bar x,\bar y)(u)=\partial^{2}f(\bar x,\bar v)(u)+\nabla^{2}g(\bar x)u.\] The sum on the right denotes translation of every element of \(\partial^{2}f(\bar x,\bar v)(u)\) by the Hessian-vector product.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a smooth function translates the second-order subdifferential by its Hessian applied to the direction.

children.title: Second-Order Convex Duality
children.top_down_role: Dual correspondence among second-order convex constructions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex duality under the half-quadratic normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(q_f=d_e^2f(x\mid v)\) and \(q_{f^*}=d_e^2f^*(v\mid x)\), where the second-order difference quotients use denominator \(\tfrac12t^2\). Then
\[
\frac12q_{f^*}=\left(\frac12q_f\right)^{\star},
\]
where \(\star\) on the right denotes Fenchel conjugation. Consequently,
\[
\partial\!\left(\frac12q_{f^*}\right)=\left[\partial\!\left(\frac12q_f\right)\right]^{-1}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At conjugate graph points, the half-scaled convex second epi-derivatives are Fenchel conjugates, so their subdifferentials are inverse relations.

The second epi-derivatives of \(f\) at \((x,v)\) and \(f^*\) at \((v,x)\) exist as proper closed convex functions under the denominator \(\tfrac12t^2\) convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tfrac12d_e^2f^*(v\mid x)=\bigl(\tfrac12d_e^2f(x\mid v)\bigr)^{\star}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(q=d_e^2f(x\mid v)\) and \(q^*=d_e^2f^*(v\mid x)\) through epi-limits of the second-order difference quotients with denominator \(\tfrac12t^2\). Then the primal and conjugate second epi-derivatives satisfy
\[
\frac12 q^*(z)=\sup_{w\in X}\left\{\langle z,w\rangle-\frac12q(w)\right\}
\quad\text{for every }z\in X.
\]
Consequently, \(\partial(\tfrac12q)\) and \(\partial(\tfrac12q^*)\) are inverse relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At conjugate primal-dual points, the half-scaled second epi-derivatives are Fenchel conjugates, and their subdifferential relations are inverses.

source_refs.locator: 4.2 Second-Order Directional Derivatives p. 162

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Although \(f\) is differentiable at \(0\) with \(f'(0)=0\), its second-order quotient in direction \(1\) is
\[
Q_t=\frac{f(t)-f(0)-t f'(0)}{\tfrac12t^2}=2\sin(1/t).
\]
Thus \(Q_t\) has no limit as \(t\downarrow0\). Removing second-order directional regularity therefore destroys the ordinary second directional derivative at the reference point; identities or chain rules requiring that derivative, twice epi-differentiability, or a compatible second-order limit are not applicable without additional hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oscillating quadratic perturbation is differentiable at zero but has no second directional derivative there, blocking calculus that requires a stable second-order limit.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is prox-regular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) if there exist \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(r\ge0\) such that
\[
f(x')\ge f(x)+\langle v,x'-x\rangle-\frac r2\lVert x'-x\rVert^2
\]
whenever \(\lVert x-\bar x\rVert<\varepsilon\), \(\lvert f(x)-f(\bar x)\rvert<\varepsilon\), \(v\in\partial f(x)\), \(\lVert v-\bar v\rVert<\varepsilon\), and \(\lVert x'-\bar x\rVert<\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prox-regularity requires nearby subgradients to support the function locally up to one uniform negative quadratic error.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a sufficiently small proximal parameter, prox-regularity yields a locally single-valued Lipschitz proximal branch.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional localized-argmin definition under linear perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\gamma>0\), define
\[
M_\gamma(v)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\|x-\bar x\|\le\gamma}\{f(x)-\langle v,x\rangle\}.
\]
The point \(\bar x\) is a tilt-stable local minimizer if, for some \(\gamma>0\), \(M_\gamma\) has a single-valued Lipschitz localization near \(v=0\) and \(M_\gamma(0)=\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tilt stability means that the localized minimizer under a small linear tilt is unique and Lipschitz in the tilt.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional prox-regular characterization using nearby attentive graph points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The point \(\bar x\) is a tilt-stable local minimizer if and only if there are \(\eta>0\) and \(c>0\) such that
\[
\langle w,u\rangle\ge c\|u\|^2
\]
for every \(u\in\mathbb R^n\), every \(w\in\partial^2f(x,v)(u)\), and every sufficiently close \(f\)-attentive graph point \((x,v)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\) satisfying \(\|(x,v)-(\bar x,0)\|<\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a prox-regular, subdifferentially continuous function, tilt stability is equivalent to uniform positive definiteness of the limiting second-order subdifferential at nearby attentive graph points.

\(0\in\partial f(\bar x)\).

\]

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are normed linear spaces, \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The neighborhood inclusion with constant \(\kappa\) defines the Aubin property at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: unit ball in the range space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighborhood Lipschitz-like property for a set-valued mapping between normed linear spaces.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) has the Aubin property at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and a constant \(\kappa\ge0\), such that
\[
F(x_1)\cap V\subset F(x_2)+\kappa\lVert x_1-x_2\rVert\mathbb B_Y
\quad\text{for all }x_1,x_2\in U.
\]
Thus every value of \(F(x_1)\) near \(\bar y\) lies within \(\kappa\lVert x_1-x_2\rVert\) of some value of \(F(x_2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Aubin property bounds the movement of every nearby localized value by a constant times the change in the input.
knowledge_statements.title: Aubin Property

children.title: Calmness
children.top_down_role: One-sided local stability of set-valued mappings relative to a reference parameter.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are metric spaces, \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The one-sided distance estimate defines calmness of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is calm at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist \(r>0\), \(s>0\), and \(\kappa\ge0\) such that
\[
d_Y(y,F(\bar x))\le \kappa d_X(x,\bar x)
\]
for every \(x\in\mathbb B_r(\bar x)\) and every \(y\in F(x)\cap\mathbb B_s(\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Calmness bounds the displacement of nearby values from the fixed reference value set by the input's distance from the reference point.
knowledge_statements.title: Calmness

children.title: Isolated Calmness
children.top_down_role: Local stability combined with isolation of the reference solution.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are metric spaces, \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed pointwise estimate defines isolated calmness and forces \(F(\bar x)\cap V=\{\bar y\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Calmness strengthened by local isolation of the reference output.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is isolatedly calm at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and \(\kappa\ge0\), such that
\[
y\in F(x)\cap V\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d_Y(y,\bar y)\le\kappa d_X(x,\bar x)
\]
for every \(x\in U\). Setting \(x=\bar x\) shows that \(F(\bar x)\cap V=\{\bar y\}\), so isolated calmness includes local uniqueness at the reference input.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Isolated calmness bounds nearby outputs directly from the reference output and consequently makes that output locally unique at the reference input.
knowledge_statements.title: Isolated Calmness

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Isolated calmness is ordinary calmness together with local isolation of the reference output in the reference value set.

children.title: Calmness Moduli
children.top_down_role: Quantitative sensitivity measures associated with calmness regimes.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are metric spaces, \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The calmness modulus is the infimum of all admissible local calmness constants.

notation.meaning: exact calmness modulus at the graph point
distance from a point to a set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact local constant for the one-sided calmness estimate.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The exact calmness modulus of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is
\[
\operatorname{clm}F(\bar x,\bar y)=\inf\left\{\kappa\ge0:\begin{array}{l}
\text{there exist neighborhoods }U\text{ of }\bar x\text{ and }V\text{ of }\bar y\text{ such that}\\
d_Y(y,F(\bar x))\le\kappa d_X(x,\bar x)\text{ for all }x\in U,\ y\in F(x)\cap V
\end{array}\right\}.
\]
The infimum is \(+\infty\) when no admissible local constant exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The calmness modulus is the infimum of the admissible one-sided local sensitivity bounds, with value infinity when the mapping is not calm.
knowledge_statements.title: Calmness Moduli

children.title: Isolation Transition Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural conditions separating ordinary calmness from solution-isolating behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R\rightrightarrows\mathbb R\) is the constant mapping \(F(x)=[-1,1]\).
The reference graph point is \((\bar x,\bar y)=(0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Calmness does not imply isolated calmness without local uniqueness of the reference value.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local uniqueness is the boundary separating calmness from isolated calmness.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\), one has \(F(x)=F(0)\), so
\[
d(y,F(0))=0\le0\lvert x\rvert
\quad\text{for every }y\in F(x).
\]
Hence \(F\) is calm at \((0,0)\) with modulus \(0\). It is not isolatedly calm there: every neighborhood \(V\) of \(0\) contains some nonzero \(y\in F(0)\cap V\), whereas isolated calmness at \(x=0\) would require \(\lvert y\rvert\le\kappa\lvert0-0\rvert=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant interval-valued mapping is calm with modulus zero but not isolatedly calm, because its reference value is not locally unique.
knowledge_statements.title: Isolation Transition Boundaries

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\). Then \(F\) is isolatedly calm at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if and only if \(F\) is calm there and \(\bar y\) is locally isolated in \(F(\bar x)\); equivalently, some neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar y\) satisfies \(F(\bar x)\cap V=\{\bar y\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Isolated calmness is exactly calmness supplemented by local isolation of the reference output in the reference value set.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are metric spaces, \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The exact local Lipschitz-like modulus of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is
\[
\operatorname{lip}F(\bar x,\bar y)=\inf\left\{\kappa\ge0:\begin{array}{l}
\text{there exist neighborhoods }U\text{ of }\bar x\text{ and }V\text{ of }\bar y\text{ such that}\\
F(x_1)\cap V\subset F(x_2)+\kappa\lVert x_1-x_2\rVert\mathbb B_Y\\
\text{for all }x_1,x_2\in U
\end{array}\right\}.
\]
Its value is \(+\infty\) if \(F\) lacks the Aubin property at the reference graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The local Lipschitz modulus is the infimum of the constants governing the Aubin inclusion near the graph point, or infinity when no such constant exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Lipschitz Moduli

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact modulus of a continuously Fréchet differentiable single-valued mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f:X\to Y\) is continuously Fréchet differentiable near \(\bar x\), then
\[
\operatorname{lip}f(\bar x)=\lVert Df(\bar x)\rVert.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuously differentiable map, the exact local Lipschitz modulus equals the operator norm of its derivative at the reference point.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are normed spaces.
\(f:X\to Y\) is continuously Fréchet differentiable on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lip}f(\bar x)=\lVert Df(\bar x)\rVert.\)

notation.meaning: Fréchet derivative of \(f\) at the reference point

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Exact-Modulus Formula

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-valued specialization of the exact local Lipschitz modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a mapping \(f:X\to Y\) defined near \(\bar x\),
\[
\operatorname{lip}f(\bar x)=\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\sup\left\{\frac{\lVert f(x)-f(x')\rVert}{\lVert x-x'\rVert}:x,x'\in B(\bar x,\delta),\ x\ne x'\right\},
\]
with value \(+\infty\) when the local quotients are unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a single-valued map, the exact local Lipschitz modulus is the limiting supremum of nearby pairwise difference quotients.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are normed spaces and \(f:X\to Y\) is defined on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle \operatorname{lip}f(\bar x)=\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\sup_{\substack{x,x'\in B(\bar x,\delta)\\x\ne x'}}\frac{\lVert f(x)-f(x')\rVert}{\lVert x-x'\rVert}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Pairwise-Quotient Representation for Single-Valued Maps

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and a constant \(\kappa\ge0\), such that
\[
d_X(x,F^{-1}(y))\le\kappa d_Y(y,F(x))
\quad\text{for every }(x,y)\in U\times V.
\]
The convention \(d(z,\varnothing)=+\infty\) is used. The least admissible \(\kappa\) is the exact regularity modulus at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric regularity bounds distance to the solution set by a uniform multiple of the residual distance near the reference graph point.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric Regularity

\((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is linearly open around \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with rate \(c>0\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and \(\varepsilon>0\), such that for every \((x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\cap(U\times V)\) and every \(r\in(0,\varepsilon)\), \[\mathbb B(y,cr)\cap V\subset F\bigl(\mathbb B(x,r)\bigr).\] The supremum of all admissible rates \(c\) is the exact linear-openness modulus at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every sufficiently small input ball centered near the reference graph point covers an output ball whose radius is at least a fixed linear multiple of the input radius.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Openness

children.top_down_role: Neighborhood coverage viewed through quantitative image inclusion.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed uniform ball inclusion is the covering property with rate \(c\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) has the local covering property around \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with rate \(c\) when there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and \(\varepsilon>0\), such that \[\mathbb B(y,ct)\cap V\subset F\bigl(\mathbb B(x,t)\bigr)\] for every \((x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\cap(U\times V)\) and every \(t\in(0,\varepsilon)\). Thus the same positive rate works uniformly at all sufficiently nearby graph points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single positive rate uniformly guarantees that small balls about nearby image points are covered by images of corresponding small domain balls.
knowledge_statements.title: Covering Properties

The conventions \(1/0=+\infty\) and \(1/(+\infty)=0\) are used.
